That means investing in community centres, in local sports facilities, in the small improvements that transform people's daily lives.

I have seen in my own constituency how a relatively modest investment in a local park can change the character of a neighbourhood. Children have somewhere safe to play. Families have a place to gather. The elderly can take their daily walks in pleasant surroundings. These are not luxuries. They are the building blocks of healthy, functioning communities.

Some will say that this spending is not prudent, that we should be more cautious with public money. I would argue the opposite. The most imprudent thing we can do is to allow our infrastructure to decay while we have the means to repair and improve it. Every year we delay is a year of lost productivity, lost opportunity, and diminished quality of life for our constituents.

The economic multiplier effect of infrastructure investment is well documented. Every pound we spend generates economic activity in construction, creates jobs, and stimulates local businesses. And once built, good infrastructure continues to pay dividends for decades. It is one of the soundest investments we can make.

I would also note that this is about fairness. For too long, infrastructure spending has been concentrated in certain favoured regions while others have been left behind. This fund represents an opportunity to correct that imbalance. Imagine what could be achieved if every community had access to similar resources. Imagine if we invested systematically in the unglamorous but essential infrastructure that determines quality of life.

The returns would extend far beyond the immediate economic impacts. Healthier communities mean lower healthcare costs. Better facilities for young people mean reduced antisocial behaviour and crime. Strong local economies mean less dependency on central government support. These investments create virtuous cycles that compound over time.

Nothing should diminish our pride in what she has accomplished thus far. From the moment she first walked into this Chamber, I knew she had that special quality that sets apart the truly great parliamentarians.

Her advocacy for her constituents has been tireless and effective. She has championed causes that others might have found too difficult or too controversial. She has stood up for the vulnerable even when it was politically inconvenient to do so. That kind of moral courage is rare, and we should celebrate it.

I have worked alongside her on several committees, and I can attest to her diligence and her mastery of detail. She does not simply show up and vote along party lines. She reads the briefing papers. She questions witnesses rigorously. She thinks independently and speaks her mind.

What I particularly admire is her willingness to work across party lines when she believes it serves the public interest. In an era of increasing polarisation, that kind of pragmatism is invaluable. She understands that good ideas can come from anywhere and that our constituents do not care about party politics when their bins are not being collected or their hospital appointments are delayed.

Of course, she and I do not agree on everything. There have been vigorous debates. But I have never doubted her sincerity or her commitment to public service. She believes in what she is doing, and she works extraordinarily hard at it. As she moves on to new responsibilities, I want to express my sincere hope that she continues to bring that same dedication and independence of mind to whatever work she undertakes next. The House will be diminished by her departure from whatever role she has been fulfilling, but I have no doubt she will continue to make valuable contributions to public life.

We need more members who approach their duties as seriously as she does. We need more willingness to work across party lines. We need more focus on substance rather than spectacle.

The people of Syria deserve better than empty words and symbolic gestures. They deserve a coordinated international response that addresses the root causes of the conflict and provides meaningful support for reconstruction and reconciliation.

We have seen too many reports from humanitarian organisations describing conditions in camps and besieged areas. Children are growing up without education, without adequate nutrition, without medical care. An entire generation is being lost while we debate the finer points of diplomatic protocols.

I am not naive about the complexities involved. The geopolitical situation is extraordinarily difficult. Multiple actors with conflicting interests are involved. Russia and Iran have their own agendas. Turkey has legitimate security concerns about its border. The various opposition groups do not speak with one voice. But complexity cannot be an excuse for inaction.

There are concrete steps we can take immediately. We can increase humanitarian funding. We can support organisations working on the ground to provide relief and document human rights abuses. We can maintain pressure on all parties to respect international humanitarian law. We can keep the issue in the public eye so that it does not fade from attention.

In the longer term, we need to be thinking about what a political settlement might look like and how we can support the Syrian people in rebuilding their country. That will require sustained engagement and significant resources. It will not be quick or easy. I recognise that achieving a political settlement will be extraordinarily difficult. The parties to the conflict have maximalist positions that seem irreconcilable. Years of violence have created deep grievances and mistrust. External actors have their own agendas that may not align with Syrian interests.

But the alternative to a political settlement is ongoing war, continued suffering, and regional instability that affects us all. We have to keep trying even when success seems distant. The Syrian people deserve no less from the international community.

The current situation is unsustainable. Congestion costs our economy billions each year in lost productivity. Carbon emissions from transport are contributing significantly to climate change. Too many people spend hours each day commuting in uncomfortable and unreliable conditions. We can and must do better.

Active travel and low carbon solutions are part of the answer, but they are not the whole answer. We need a comprehensive strategy that recognises different people have different needs. A parent with young children cannot necessarily cycle to the shops. Someone with mobility issues needs accessible public transport. A tradesperson needs to transport tools and materials.

What I want to see is a transport network that gives people genuine choices. That means frequent, reliable, affordable public transport. It means safe cycling infrastructure that is separated from traffic. It means well-maintained pavements. It means careful planning so that new developments are built with transport in mind rather than as an afterthought.

Bus reform is particularly important. The current fragmented system does not serve passengers well. Routes are designed around commercial considerations rather than passenger needs. Timetables are not coordinated. Ticketing is confusing and expensive. Other cities have shown that bringing buses back under public control can transform the service. bringing buses under democratic control has improved frequency, lowered fares, and created integrated networks that people actually want to use. There is no technical barrier to doing the same here. The barrier is political will and ideological commitment to privatisation regardless of outcomes.

I would urge the combined authority to be ambitious in its vision and in its proposals. Incremental tinkering will not solve the deep-rooted problems we face. We need transformational change in how we think about and provide transport.

This is a matter of national memory and collective conscience. As the generation that experienced these events firsthand passes away, we have a responsibility to ensure that their testimony is preserved and that future generations understand what happened and why it must never happen again.

The creeping normalisation of extreme views is something we must actively resist. It happens gradually. A joke that would once have been unthinkable becomes acceptable. A conspiracy theory gains traction. Historical facts are disputed or distorted. Before we know it, ideas that were once confined to the fringes have entered mainstream discourse.

Education is our most powerful tool. Young people need to learn not just the historical facts but also how to think critically about the sources of information they encounter. They need to understand how propaganda works, how prejudice develops, how ordinary people can be led to commit or tolerate atrocities.

This law is not about restricting legitimate historical debate or academic inquiry. It is about drawing a clear line against deliberate denial and distortion. There is a difference between questioning specific aspects of the historical record and denying that the Holocaust occurred. The former is scholarship. The latter is propaganda designed to rehabilitate fascism.

Some will argue that the best response to bad speech is more speech rather than legal sanction. I have sympathy with that view in general, but Holocaust denial is a special case. Holocaust denial exists in a category with very few other forms of speech. It is not a good-faith attempt to understand history. It is a deliberate lie told in service of a hateful ideology. Treating it as ordinary speech that should be countered with more speech misunderstands its nature and its purpose.

The law recognises that some forms of speech cause direct harm and serve no legitimate purpose. This is one of them. By drawing that line clearly, we reaffirm our commitment to human dignity and to historical truth.

He embodied a particular kind of public service that is increasingly rare. He did not seek the spotlight. He did not give interviews about his feelings or write memoirs settling scores. He simply got on with the job, year after year, decade after decade, supporting the Queen and representing our country with dignity and distinction.

His legacy is visible in the numerous organisations and charities he founded or supported. The Duke of Edinburgh's Award has transformed millions of young lives, building confidence and resilience. His environmental work was ahead of its time. His championing of engineering and design helped elevate those fields in public esteem.

What struck me most on the occasions I met him was his genuine curiosity. He asked probing questions. He wanted to understand how things worked. He did not suffer fools, but he respected expertise and listened to those who knew what they were talking about.

In my constituency, we have a youth centre that received support through one of his charities. I have seen personally the difference it makes to young people from disadvantaged backgrounds. They gain skills, build friendships, develop a sense of purpose. That is a living legacy that will continue long after the formal mourning period has ended.

We live in an age that is often cynical about institutions and sceptical of traditional authority. Prince Philip represented something that transcends partisan politics. values that are under pressure in our modern age. Duty, service, putting something larger than oneself first. These are qualities we desperately need, and his example reminds us that they are possible and valuable.

I believe the outpouring of grief and respect we have seen reflects not just affection for Prince Philip personally but also a recognition that something important has been lost and will not easily be replaced.

That moment crystallised something profound about our responsibility as educators and as a society. We cannot simply lecture young people about reconciliation and respect for different cultures if we do not create genuine opportunities for them to engage with difficult history and painful truths.

The picture was not just an historical artifact. It represented real people who suffered real harm. It represented systems of oppression that have ongoing effects today. And it represented a failure of imagination and empathy on the part of those who did not immediately see why it was problematic.

What my son experienced in that room is what indigenous young people experience constantly. They see their history misrepresented or ignored. They see their pain minimised. They see non-indigenous people making decisions about how to address issues that affect indigenous communities, often without meaningful consultation or genuine listening.

This is why reconciliation cannot just be a buzzword or a box to tick. It requires deep structural change in how we educate, how we make policy, how we allocate resources. It requires those of us with privilege and power to step back and create space for indigenous voices and indigenous leadership.

I want to be clear that this is not about guilt or blame. It is about responsibility and action. We did not create the systems that led to residential schools and intergenerational trauma, but we benefit from them, and we have a duty to work toward repair. My son's experience is not unique. It is shared by countless indigenous young people across this country. They sit in rooms where decisions are made about them, not with them. They watch their experiences be misunderstood or minimised. They carry pain that others do not even recognise.

Until we fundamentally change that dynamic, until we genuinely share power and truly listen, reconciliation will remain an aspiration rather than a reality. And that would be a failure we all bear responsibility for.

We are looking at the facts and proposing practical solutions based on evidence rather than ideology. The reality is that certain decisions made at Westminster have profound effects on Scotland, and Scottish people deserve to have a meaningful say in those decisions.

This is not about special treatment. It is about basic democratic principles. When policies affect devolved areas, there should be genuine consultation and, where appropriate, consent from the devolved administrations. That is not a veto. It is respectful partnership in a union that is supposed to be voluntary and mutually beneficial.

I am weary of being told that any defence of Scotland's interests amounts to nationalism or separatism. It is possible to want to remain in the union while also insisting that the union be reformed to work better for all its constituent parts. In fact, that is the position of most Scottish voters.

The alternative being offered is a take-it-or-leave-it approach where Westminster imposes decisions regardless of Scottish opinion. That is not sustainable. It breeds resentment and undermines support for the union far more effectively than any independence campaign could.

What we need is grown-up conversation about how power should be distributed in a modern multinational state. Other countries manage this. Federal systems exist and function well. There is no reason we cannot develop structures that respect both the integrity of the union and the distinct democratic mandates of its component nations. The current approach treats Scotland as subordinate rather than as an equal partner. That is not consistent with the rhetoric about a family of nations or a voluntary union. If the union is to survive and thrive, it needs to be based on genuine partnership and mutual respect, not on one party imposing its will on the others.

This is not about Scottish exceptionalism. It is about basic fairness and workable governance. If we cannot find ways to accommodate legitimate concerns from Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the union will continue to fracture.

That scheme represented our recognition that parenting is not just a private responsibility but something society as a whole should support. Single parents in particular face extraordinary challenges. They are trying to provide economically for their children while also being present to care for them. Without affordable childcare, that becomes impossible.

I have met single mothers in my constituency who are working multiple part-time jobs, struggling to coordinate childcare, exhausted and stressed. These are not people looking for handouts. They are working hard and doing their best. What they need is a system that does not penalise them for doing the right thing.

The economic case for affordable childcare is overwhelming. When parents, especially mothers, can participate fully in the workforce, that generates tax revenue and reduces dependence on benefits. When children receive quality early education, that improves outcomes across their lifetimes. This is investment, not expenditure.

But beyond economics, there is a moral dimension. We say we value children and families. We say we believe in opportunity and social mobility. Those values are hollow if we do not back them up with resources. If quality childcare is available only to the wealthy, we are perpetuating inequality across generations.

The full scheme will take time to implement properly. I understand that. But we need to be moving forward with urgency. The full implementation will take time, I understand that. But we need to see urgency and we need to see progress. Too many families have been waiting too long. Too many children are missing out on opportunities because their parents cannot afford childcare.

This scheme could be transformative if it is implemented properly and at scale. I will continue to press for that and to hold the Government accountable for delivering on the commitments that have been made.

This is not peripheral to the Department's remit. Children are affected by every aspect of government policy. Intercountry adoption involves complex questions about child welfare, identity, and family relationships. Education is fundamental to how children develop and what opportunities they have access to.

If we are serious about putting children at the centre of policymaking, we cannot have major legislation moving forward that does not consider impacts on children and young people. That is not just about adding a clause here or there. It is about fundamentally thinking through how different provisions will work in practice for actual children in specific situations.

I am particularly concerned about intercountry adoption because of the potential for unintended consequences. Changes to how we process and recognise adoptions from other countries could create enormous uncertainty for families in the middle of the process. There are already significant delays and bureaucratic hurdles. We cannot make those worse through poorly drafted legislation.

Education transitions are another critical area. Children who are adopted often have experienced trauma and disruption. Stability in schooling is essential for their wellbeing and development. If this Bill creates barriers or complications, that could have serious effects that we should anticipate and address now rather than discovering them after implementation.

I appreciate that the Minister has other priorities. I understand that coordinating across multiple departments is complex. But that is exactly why we have parliamentary scrutiny. This Bill needs to get it right for children. They cannot advocate for themselves in this chamber. They depend on us to think through implications and to protect their interests. That is a responsibility I take seriously and I hope all members do as well.

I would urge the Government to go back, to consult specifically with the Department of Children and Youth Affairs, to think through these issues carefully, and to come back with provisions that actually address the concerns rather than creating new problems.

I am disappointed because I believe we could and should be doing better. The school in question serves a community that has been patient and cooperative throughout a difficult process. They were given assurances that have not been met. They have been asked to wait and wait again. That is not acceptable.

This is not the first time we have had this conversation. The Minister and I have discussed this school before. Progress was promised. Timelines were set. And yet here we are again, with continued delays and inadequate explanations. At some point, promises need to turn into action.

The children in this school deserve the same quality facilities as children in more affluent areas. The teachers deserve to work in a building that is fit for purpose. The parents deserve to know that their children are being educated in a safe, modern environment. These are not unreasonable expectations.

I know the Minister will point to budget constraints and competing priorities. I understand those pressures. But I also know that when there is political will, solutions can be found. Other projects move forward quickly when they are deemed important. This school should be important too.

What I want from the Minister today is not another vague commitment to move things forward. I want a concrete timeline with specific milestones. I want an explanation of what exactly has been causing the delays. I want specific dates. I want named responsible parties. I want triggers for escalation if milestones are not met. Without that kind of concrete accountability, I fear we will be having this exact same conversation in another six months or a year.

The children of this school have already waited long enough. They deserve action, not more promises. I will continue to press on this issue until the school gets what it needs and what it was promised.

That would create additional hardship for people who are already in an incredibly vulnerable position. These homeowners did not cause the financial crisis. They have been making their payments to the best of their ability. They have worked with the banks in good faith. To now threaten them with homelessness would be unconscionable.

We have a responsibility to protect people from the worst excesses of the market. That is what government is for. The banks made risky lending decisions during the boom. They profited handsomely. When the crash came, they were bailed out with public money. The least we can do is ensure that ordinary families are not sacrificed to protect bank balance sheets.

There are workable solutions available. We can extend restructuring arrangements. We can provide support for those at risk of losing their homes. We can ensure that repossessions are truly a last resort after all other options have been exhausted. These measures are not radical. They are humane and practical.

The social cost of homelessness far exceeds any short-term financial consideration. Families torn apart. Children's education disrupted. Mental health crises. Increased demand for emergency accommodation and social services. It is both morally wrong and economically foolish to allow this to happen when we have the power to prevent it.

I am calling on the Taoiseach to stand with the people on this issue. I stand with the people, not with the banks. I stand with families trying to keep their homes, not with institutions trying to maximise profits. I believe the Taoiseach should too, and I hope the Government will act accordingly to protect vulnerable homeowners from the threat of homelessness.

The parish has done everything right. They engaged with the planning process in good faith. They consulted widely within their community. They made difficult decisions about which sites to allocate. They produced a plan that balanced development needs with environmental protection and community character.

And now they face the prospect of that plan being undermined or overridden because the system does not adequately protect neighbourhood plans from subsequent challenges. That is deeply unfair and it undermines trust in the entire planning system.

If we want local communities to engage meaningfully in planning, they need to know that their efforts will be respected. They need confidence that a neighbourhood plan, once adopted, will carry real weight. Otherwise, why would anyone invest the time and energy required to produce one?

The Bill should strengthen protections for neighbourhood plans. It should make clear that once a community has gone through the process and allocated sites, developers cannot simply ignore that and propose alternatives. There should be a strong presumption in favour of the community's plan unless there are exceptional circumstances.

This is also about capacity. Larger developers have resources to navigate the planning system, to hire consultants, to mount legal challenges. Small communities do not have those resources. The system should not favour those with the deepest pockets. The community should have the confidence that when they produce a neighbourhood plan through the proper process, it will be respected. Developers should know that they need to work within the framework the community has established rather than trying to circumvent it.

Strengthening these protections is not anti-development. It is pro-democracy and pro-good planning. When communities are confident their voice matters, they engage more constructively with necessary development. When they feel their participation is meaningless, that breeds opposition to everything.

Parents in rural areas are already dealing with limited services and long distances to access education and healthcare. Transport should not be another source of stress and confusion. There should be clear, consistent rules that apply across all school transport services.

I understand that different schools have different circumstances. Some are dealing with multiple routes. Some have capacity constraints. But from a parent's perspective, the inconsistency is baffling and frustrating. Why can children from one school share transport but not children from another? Why are some families told there is space while others are turned away?

This is fundamentally about fairness and access to education. If children cannot get to school reliably and affordably, their education suffers. This particularly affects families in remote areas who may have no alternative. They cannot drive their children because of work commitments or because they do not have a vehicle. There is no public transport option. School transport is not a luxury for them. It is essential.

I would urge the Minister to conduct a comprehensive review of how school transport is allocated and managed. We need clear national guidelines that ensure consistency and fairness. We need adequate funding so that services are not being cut or restricted. And we need better communication with families so they understand what to expect. In the meantime, what I want from the Minister is acknowledgment of the problem, commitment to addressing it, and concrete action to ensure consistent, fair rules for school transport across all schools and all areas.

Parents should not have to navigate a confusing patchwork of different policies. Children should not miss out on education because of transport barriers. This is basic but essential.

The House must call upon the Prime Minister to take responsibility for what happened in his office and under his watch. These are not abstract questions about procedural propriety. They involve real people who experienced harassment and whose concerns were allegedly not addressed appropriately.

Leadership means creating a workplace culture where people feel safe to report problems and confident that those problems will be taken seriously. Leadership means holding oneself and one's staff to high standards of conduct. Leadership means accepting responsibility when things go wrong rather than deflecting or denying.

If the Prime Minister was not aware of the allegation, that itself raises serious questions about how his office was being managed. A senior staff member facing a serious allegation should have been something the Prime Minister knew about. The fact that he apparently did not suggests either that he was not being properly briefed or that there were deliberate efforts to keep him in the dark. Neither is acceptable.

If he was aware and did not act, that is even more serious. It would mean consciously choosing to ignore an allegation of sexual harassment. That would be a fundamental failure of duty and would make his previous statements about zero tolerance for such behaviour ring hollow.

The standard we walk past is the standard we accept. That principle applies with even greater force to those in positions of authority. We need answers, not deflection. We need accountability, not excuses. And if those at the top failed to create a safe workplace or failed to act on reports of harassment, there need to be consequences.

The victims of harassment deserve justice. The public deserves to know that their leaders are being held to appropriate standards. This House deserves leadership that takes these issues seriously and acts with integrity.

I do think we need to be realistic about what that changed position will look like. Some businesses will have different operating models. Some sectors will have contracted while others will have grown. Some ways of working that we adapted to during the crisis may become permanent.

The goal should not be to simply restore the pre-crisis status quo. We should be asking what kind of economy and society we want to build as we recover. This is an opportunity to address longstanding problems and to make choices that create a fairer, more sustainable, more resilient future.

For individuals, same position might mean the same job, but it could also mean a different job at comparable pay and conditions. For many workers, the crisis has been devastating. Jobs lost, savings depleted, career progression halted. Our support needs to recognise that recovery is not instantaneous.

For companies, same position means being able to continue operating and serving customers. But that might look different than it did before. Some have had to pivot their business models. Some have discovered that remote work is viable. Some have streamlined operations. The government support should enable survival and adaptation, not preserve inefficiency.

What concerns me is the gap between the principle and the implementation. The schemes announced have been helpful for many, but they have also had significant gaps. We need to think about what kind of recovery we want, not just accept whatever emerges. We need to build back better, as the phrase goes, though that requires moving beyond slogans to actual policy.

For individuals and for companies, the goal should be fair, sustainable outcomes that reflect both support through crisis and adaptation to changed circumstances. That requires judgment and flexibility, not rigid formulas.

SACE provides crisis intervention, counselling, and support for survivors of sexual assault. They operate a 24-hour crisis line. They accompany survivors to medical appointments and court proceedings. They deliver education programs to prevent sexual violence. This is difficult, essential work that saves lives and helps people heal from trauma.

I want to particularly acknowledge the volunteers. These are people who give their time because they believe in the mission and want to help their community. They undergo extensive training. They provide emotional support to people going through the worst experiences of their lives. They do this without expectation of payment or recognition.

Sexual violence is a pervasive problem that affects people of all backgrounds. The statistics are sobering. Too many women, and men as well, have experienced assault or harassment. Too many survivors suffer in silence because they fear they will not be believed or that nothing will be done.

Organisations like SACE are critical to changing that. They provide a safe place where survivors can talk about what happened to them. They help survivors understand that what happened was not their fault. They navigate systems that can be intimidating and retraumatising. They advocate for better policies and practices.

In my time representing Edmonton Centre, I have seen the impact of SACE's work firsthand. They have met survivors at their most vulnerable moments. They have helped them navigate a process that can be retraumatising. They have been there when no one else was. That dedication deserves our recognition and our support.

We need to ensure SACE and similar organisations have the resources they need to continue this vital work. Sexual violence is not going away. The need for these services will continue. We have a responsibility to fund them adequately and to support the staff and volunteers who do this difficult work.

I must put these questions to the House without further debate, in accordance with our Standing Orders. Each question will be put separately. Members will indicate their position by rising in their places or through the remote voting system as appropriate.

I want to thank all members who have participated in this debate. The diversity of views expressed reflects the importance of these fiscal measures to our constituents and to the country as a whole. While we may disagree on specifics, I trust that all members are motivated by a genuine desire to serve the public interest.

Let me remind the House that these Ways and Means motions provide the necessary fiscal authority for the measures contained in the Finance Bill. They are essential to implementing the budget that was presented and debated extensively. A vote against these motions would create significant uncertainty and disruption.

I would also note for the record that the extensive debate we have had over recent days has allowed ample opportunity for scrutiny and amendment. The government has listened to concerns and made adjustments where appropriate. The process has worked as it should.

Now we must move to decision. I will put each motion in turn. Members should listen carefully and vote according to their conscience and their assessment of what best serves their constituents. These motions have been debated extensively over recent weeks. Members have had ample opportunity to express their views, to propose amendments, to scrutinise the details. Now it is time to vote and to move forward with implementing the budget.

I remind all members that your votes today will be recorded and will be a matter of public record. Your constituents will see how you voted on these important fiscal measures. Vote according to your conscience and your judgment of what best serves the public interest.

There are many people with similar experiences, and their stories are painful and important. But we need to be careful about how we represent their views and what we claim on their behalf. Different survivors have different perspectives on what would be helpful or healing.

Some want public inquiries and formal processes. Others want privacy and to be left alone. Some want financial compensation. Others want reforms to prevent future harm. Some want specific individuals held accountable. Others want to focus on systemic change rather than individual blame.

It is not appropriate for any politician to declare themselves the singular voice for such a diverse group. We can listen. We can advocate. We can push for action. But we should not claim to speak for people without their explicit consent and involvement.

This is particularly important when the issues are traumatic and sensitive. We need to be guided by what survivors themselves say they need, not by what we think they should need or what would be politically convenient. That requires ongoing dialogue and genuine partnership rather than assumptions.

I have concerns about how this matter has been handled politically. There has been a tendency to use survivors' experiences as ammunition in partisan battles. That is disrespectful and it risks reducing complex human experiences to talking points.

What I want to see is less grandstanding and more genuine engagement with the difficult questions. What survivors need is to be heard on their own terms and to have their specific requests and needs addressed. Different people will have different priorities. Some want acknowledgment. Some want compensation. Some want reform. Some want all of these things.

Our job is to listen, to create space for their voices, and to respond appropriately to what they tell us they need. It is not to assume we know what is best or to use their experiences to score political points.

Many people in rural Ireland and in underserved urban areas have been waiting for years for adequate broadband connectivity. This is not a luxury. It is essential infrastructure for participating in the modern economy, accessing education and healthcare, and connecting with family and friends.

The delays in the national broadband plan have been frustrating for everyone. There have been process issues, there have been bidder withdrawals, there have been cost escalations. I understand why people are sceptical about whether it will ever actually be delivered.

But the need has not gone away. If anything, it has become more acute. The pandemic demonstrated how vital reliable internet access is. People working from home. Children learning remotely. Medical consultations conducted online. All of this requires broadband that many of my constituents simply do not have.

I appreciate that the Minister is relatively new to the portfolio, but this issue predates his tenure and will outlast it unless we finally get it resolved. We need a clear timeline for rollout. We need transparency about what is happening and why there are delays. We need accountability when commitments are not met.

There are areas where people are still using dial-up internet or expensive and unreliable mobile data. Businesses cannot operate. Young people cannot access educational resources. The reality on the ground in rural Ireland is that many people simply cannot participate in modern life without decent broadband. They cannot work from home. Their children cannot access online educational resources. They cannot use basic government services that have moved online.

This is creating a two-tier society where urban areas have access to opportunities and services that rural areas do not. That is not acceptable in a modern democracy. We need to bridge that digital divide urgently.

Last week, something quite remarkable happened during these proceedings. The Financial Times and other reputable outlets reported on aspects of the case that raised new questions and cast doubt on certain claims that had been presented as fact.

What was curious was not that new information emerged. That happens in complex cases. What was curious was the response, or rather the lack of response. Points that should have been addressed were not. Questions that demanded answers received only silence or deflection.

This has created an unsatisfactory situation where we are being asked to proceed on the basis of an incomplete picture. Parliament functions on the principle that members are provided with accurate information. When that information is called into doubt, there should be clarification. When witnesses' accounts are questioned, there should be opportunity for scrutiny.

I am not suggesting bad faith on anyone's part. But I am suggesting that we have a procedural problem that needs to be resolved before we continue. If the article's claims are incorrect, that should be easy to demonstrate. If they are correct, or partially correct, then we need to understand what that means for our proceedings.

David Allen Green is not a partisan commentator. He is a serious legal analyst with a track record of careful reporting. His observation that something curious happened is not something we should simply brush aside. David Allen Green's observation that something curious happened deserves serious attention and response. This Parliament deserves clarity. The public deserves to have confidence in our proceedings.

I hope the matter will be addressed properly so we can proceed with full understanding of what actually occurred and what it means for the case before us.

Mental health has been the hidden crisis of the pandemic. We have rightly focused on the direct health impacts of the virus and on the economic consequences. But the mental health toll has been enormous and it will persist long after the acute phase of the pandemic has passed.

Isolation, anxiety, bereavement, financial stress, disruption to routines and support systems. All of these have taken a psychological toll. Young people have missed crucial developmental experiences. Healthcare workers are experiencing burnout and trauma. Families have been dealing with extraordinary pressures.

The challenge now is to ensure that mental health services are resourced to meet the surge in demand that is already becoming apparent. Waiting lists for therapy and counselling are growing. School counsellors are overwhelmed. Crisis services are stretched.

We cannot allow mental health to remain the poor relation in our health system. Parity of esteem between mental and physical health is not just a slogan. It requires investment in services, in training, in research, in prevention. in prevention and in early intervention. We need to create a society where mental health is treated as seriously as physical health, where people feel able to seek help without stigma, where support is available when and where it is needed.

The mental health first aid programme my hon. Friend has launched in Watford is an excellent model. I hope other constituencies will adopt similar approaches. This is exactly the kind of community-based initiative that can make a real difference.

The House should not be misled about what the Chancellor said or the basis on which decisions were made. Accuracy in ministerial statements is not a technical nicety. It is fundamental to how this House functions and how we hold the executive to account.

If the Chancellor did mislead, even inadvertently, that should be corrected at the earliest opportunity. If he did not mislead, then the concerns raised should be addressed directly so that the record is clear. What we cannot have is ambiguity on matters of fact that are central to major policy decisions.

The ACAS report is publicly funded, as I mentioned. It was commissioned to provide independent analysis of a contentious employment practice. The findings should be in the public domain. There may be specific details that need to be redacted for privacy or commercial reasons, but the substance should be available.

The refusal to release the report raises questions about what it contains and whether it contradicts the government's stated position. If the report supports the government's approach, why not publish it? If it raises concerns, why not address those concerns openly?

This pattern of withholding information while making policy claims is troubling. Parliament cannot effectively scrutinise legislation if we do not have access to the evidence base. Parliament deserves the truth. If the Chancellor made statements that were inaccurate, that should be corrected. If the ACAS report contains findings that contradict government claims, that should be acknowledged. Transparency is not optional. It is essential to democratic accountability.

I will continue to press for release of the report and for clarification of the discrepancies that have been raised. This is too important to let slide.

Recruiting additional GPs to rural areas has been a longstanding challenge. The workload is heavy. The on-call commitments are demanding. The professional isolation can be difficult. Younger doctors, understandably, are attracted to urban practices where they have colleagues nearby and better work-life balance.

But the consequence is that rural communities end up underserved. Appointment waiting times are longer. Patients have difficulty accessing care when they need it. The existing doctors face burnout. It becomes a vicious cycle where the challenges of the practice make recruitment even harder.

We need a comprehensive rural health strategy that addresses these issues. That might include financial incentives for doctors willing to work in underserved areas. It might include better use of technology to provide remote consultations and share expertise. It might include different staffing models that allow practices to share resources.

What is not sustainable is the current situation where we simply hope that enough doctors will choose to work in rural areas out of a sense of vocation. We need creative solutions, not just hope. We need incentives that actually work. We need support structures that make rural practice sustainable. And we need to ensure that when we invest public money in training doctors, there is some expectation that they will serve the communities that need them, not just flock to the most attractive locations.

This is a challenge that requires sustained attention and investment, not just periodic expressions of concern.

The Bill asks us to confront one of the most profound questions a society can face. Under what circumstances, if any, should we permit individuals to end their own lives with medical assistance? This is not a question we should answer lightly or quickly.

I have deep respect for those on both sides of this debate. There are people of good faith who believe that compassion requires allowing those who are suffering to choose a dignified death. There are equally people of good faith who believe that legalising assisted dying would put vulnerable people at risk and undermine the principle that all life has value.

My own view is shaped by concerns about safeguards and about the message this sends about the value of disabled lives. I worry about subtle pressures that could be placed on people who feel they are a burden. I worry about the adequacy of palliative care and whether we are offering genuine choice if pain management is inadequate.

But I also recognise the powerful testimony of those who have watched loved ones die in distress and who desperately wanted to be able to help them end their suffering. I recognise that there are limits to what palliative care can achieve. I recognise the force of the autonomy argument.

This is the kind of question that deserves extensive consultation. This deserves the most careful deliberation we can give it. We should take time to hear from experts, from those with terminal illnesses, from disability rights advocates, from palliative care providers, from ethicists and legal scholars. We should examine evidence from jurisdictions that have legalised assisted dying.

And then we should vote according to our conscience, recognising the profound weight of the decision we are making.

There is a balance to be struck. We absolutely must protect trafficking victims who have been brought here against their will and exploited. They need support and safety, not deportation. Many have experienced horrific abuse. They deserve compassion and justice.

What is not acceptable is a situation where serious criminals are able to evade justice by making false trafficking claims. That brings the entire system into disrepute and it creates a perverse incentive structure. We need to close that loophole while maintaining protection for those who genuinely need it. genuine trafficking victims who have experienced horrific abuse deserve our protection and support. They should not have that protection diminished because the system is being gamed by others.

The challenge is getting the balance right. We need robust systems to identify false claims without creating barriers that prevent genuine victims from getting help. We need fast processing so people are not left in limbo. We need consequences for those who abuse the system.

This is difficult but essential work. Our modern slavery legislation was groundbreaking and important. We need to ensure it is used properly.

Traffic fatalities are preventable. Every death on our roads is a tragedy that leaves families devastated and communities grieving. Distracted driving is one of the leading causes, and it is entirely within our power to address.

The statistics I cited are stark. More than one quarter of all crash fatalities. Seventy-eight deaths per year on average. Those are not just numbers. Those are parents, children, friends, colleagues. Those are people who would still be alive if someone had simply put down their phone.

We have made progress on drunk driving through a combination of laws, enforcement, and cultural change. There is now broad social consensus that driving under the influence is unacceptable. We need to create the same cultural shift around distracted driving.

Young people in particular need to understand the risks. For many, their phones are almost an extension of themselves. The idea of not responding to a text immediately feels unnatural. But when you are driving, that text can wait. It is not worth someone's life.

Enforcement is part of the answer. Penalties need to be significant enough to deter the behaviour. But enforcement alone is not enough. We need public education campaigns. We need technology solutions that make it harder to use phones while driving. The technology exists to make this easier. Cars can be designed with systems that disable phone functions while driving. Phones can detect when they are in a moving vehicle and restrict use. These solutions are available. We should be deploying them.

Ultimately, this is about valuing human life. Every death from distracted driving is preventable. Every family that loses someone to this entirely avoidable cause deserves better from us. We have the knowledge and the tools to address this problem. What we need is the will to act.

These issues have been very much at the forefront of government thinking. We have had numerous internal discussions at cabinet level and within the parliamentary party. Deputies from affected areas have made their concerns very clear. We understand the urgency.

The challenge is balancing multiple competing priorities within constrained resources. Everyone wants their area to receive investment and attention. Every issue seems urgent to those directly affected. Government requires making difficult choices about sequencing and resource allocation.

What I can say is that this issue is not being ignored. Work is ongoing. Officials are engaged with stakeholders. Options are being developed and evaluated. But I cannot provide a timeline because I do not want to make commitments that might not be met. That has happened too often in the past and it erodes trust.

I would rather under-promise and over-deliver than create expectations that cannot be fulfilled. I recognise that this is frustrating for Deputy Griffin and for others who are looking for concrete action. But the alternative is making announcements that sound good but do not translate into results.

What I can commit to is continued engagement. The Deputy has been constructive in how he has raised these concerns. The Deputy can count on my engagement and on serious consideration of the issues raised. I may not always be able to give the answers or timelines that are wanted, but I will always listen and I will always take the concerns seriously.

That is the best I can offer, and I hope it is sufficient for us to work together constructively on these important matters.

Some degree of warming is now locked in because of emissions that have already occurred. Even if we stopped all emissions tomorrow, which we cannot and will not, there would still be warming because of the greenhouse gases already in the atmosphere. That is the physical reality.

So we have two parallel tasks. Mitigation: reducing emissions as rapidly as possible to limit future warming. And adaptation: preparing for and responding to the climate impacts that are already happening and will continue to happen.

Both are necessary. We cannot adapt our way out of runaway climate change. There are tipping points beyond which adaptation becomes impossible. But equally, we cannot mitigate fast enough to prevent all impacts, so adaptation is essential for protecting communities and ecosystems.

The challenge is that adaptation is expensive and difficult. It requires infrastructure investments, changes to planning and building codes, support for affected communities. And there is always a temptation to delay because the impacts feel distant or because other priorities seem more urgent. The challenge is deciding how much adaptation to pursue for different scenarios. We cannot afford to adapt to every possible climate future. We need to make decisions about which risks to prioritise, which investments to make, which communities and systems to protect first.

Those are difficult choices with major distributional implications. Some regions and populations are more vulnerable than others. Some have more resources to adapt. Justice and equity need to be central to how we approach adaptation, not afterthoughts.

The people of Longford have shown remarkable resilience and solidarity in the face of these challenges. They have supported each other. They have worked with the Gardaí. They have refused to be intimidated. That community spirit is admirable and it deserves to be supported.

The Minister mentioned the 7,000 incidents, which is a staggering number for a town of Longford's size. That gives a sense of the scale of the problem. It is not a few isolated incidents. It is sustained criminal activity that has affected the entire community.

What people want to know is what happens next. The operation has been running since 2019. There have been incidents and arrests. But people do not feel that the underlying problem has been solved. They still do not feel safe in their own community.

I think we need to look beyond enforcement alone. Law enforcement is essential and I commend the Gardaí for their work. But we also need to address root causes. Why is there such a concentration of criminal activity in Longford? What socioeconomic factors are contributing? What can be done to prevent young people from being drawn into criminality?

These are difficult questions without easy answers. But we also need to be honest about the fact that law enforcement alone will not solve this problem. We need economic development. We need education and opportunity. We need alternatives for young people who might otherwise be drawn into criminal activity.

The people of Longford deserve both immediate security and long-term investment in their community's future. Both are necessary. Neither alone is sufficient.

She broke barriers at a time when that required extraordinary courage and determination. As the first Black graduate from that nursing school, she faced discrimination and obstacles that we can barely imagine today. Yet she persevered, excelled, and went on to lead.

Her legacy is not just her personal achievements, though those are remarkable. Her legacy is the path she created for others. Every Black nurse who came after her benefited from her trailblazing. Every student who saw her leadership knew that they too could aspire to leadership.

Cape Breton is rightly proud of her, as we all should be. She embodied the best values of public service: dedication to helping others, commitment to excellence, willingness to challenge injustice. She made her community and her profession better.

As we mourn her passing, we should also celebrate her life and ensure that her story is told and remembered. Too often, the contributions of Black Canadians and other minority communities are forgotten or minimised. We have a responsibility to preserve and honour these histories.

I would encourage the community in Cape Breton to find ways to memorialise Clotilda Douglas-Yakimchuk's legacy. Perhaps a scholarship in her name. Perhaps a community health initiative. Perhaps naming a nursing scholarship or a community health facility in her honour. Perhaps sharing her story in schools so young people know about her pioneering work. Perhaps celebrating her in ways that ensure her contributions are not forgotten.

She deserves to be remembered and celebrated. And we have a responsibility to ensure that happens.

It is a transparent attempt to undermine the government's negotiating position and to create doubt about the benefits of leaving the European Union. The timing is not coincidental. This analysis has been leaked at a moment designed to cause maximum political damage.

We should be clear about what this analysis is and what it is not. It is one preliminary assessment based on certain assumptions. It is not the final word on what the economic impacts will be. Economic modelling is inherently uncertain, especially when dealing with unprecedented changes.

Moreover, the analysis appears to focus only on costs and not on benefits. It does not account for the opportunities that will arise from being able to set our own trade policy, regulate our own industries, control our own borders. It presents a partial and pessimistic picture.

I am not suggesting that there will be no challenges or adjustments. Of course there will be. Any significant change creates winners and losers, costs and benefits. But the British people voted for this change with their eyes open. They understood that there might be short-term disruption in pursuit of long-term sovereignty.

The government is undertaking comprehensive analysis of the impacts of different exit scenarios. That analysis will inform our negotiations and our preparations. That work is being done by civil servants and by ministers. But we cannot share all the details publicly while negotiations are ongoing. That would undermine our negotiating position and make it harder to achieve a good outcome.

What I can say is that the analysis will inform our decisions and that we are committed to protecting British interests while pursuing the best possible relationship with the EU as we leave.

We have fought tooth and nail to protect the Irish fishing sector at every stage of these negotiations. We have made clear how important the fishing industry is to coastal communities, to employment, to our maritime heritage. We have rejected proposals that would have undermined our interests.

It might be easy for others to criticise from the sidelines, but the reality is that we are negotiating with partners who have their own interests and their own priorities. The UK in particular has taken a very hardline position on fishing. The Commission has had to balance the interests of multiple member states.

Ireland has been well represented in those negotiations. Our officials and ministers have been forceful advocates. We have achieved protection for important fisheries. We have secured continued access to waters that matter to our fleet. Have we gotten everything we wanted? No. But we have done significantly better than some of the doomsday scenarios predicted.

What I would say to Deputy is that criticism is easy but alternatives are hard. It is not enough to say we should have fought harder. The question is: fought for what, specifically? What exactly should we have done differently? What would the Deputy have demanded that we did not demand? Have we achieved everything? No. Could we have achieved more? Perhaps, though I would challenge anyone to specify exactly how given the constraints we faced. But we have achieved significant protection for Irish fishing interests and we have done so by being forceful advocates at every stage.

That is the reality, whatever critics from the sidelines may claim.

We have consistently said that a UK-wide approach is our first preference. That makes sense for many reasons. It simplifies compliance for businesses. It provides consistency for citizens. It reflects the fact that we are one country with shared institutions and common interests.

The protocol exists because a UK-wide solution was not available for certain aspects of EU withdrawal. The unique circumstances of Northern Ireland, the land border with an EU member state, the sensitivity around the Good Friday Agreement, all of this meant that a bespoke arrangement was necessary.

But that does not mean we should default to bespoke arrangements in other areas where they are not necessary. We should always ask first whether a UK-wide approach can work. Only when that is genuinely not feasible should we consider something different for Northern Ireland.

This is important for maintaining the integrity of the United Kingdom. Northern Ireland is part of the UK. Its citizens should have the same rights and be subject to the same laws as citizens in other parts of the UK, except where there are compelling reasons for differentiation.

At the same time, we have to be realistic about the consequences of the protocol. It does create some regulatory divergence. It does mean that Northern Ireland has a different relationship with the EU than other parts of the UK. At the same time, we need to be pragmatic about the fact that some degree of divergence exists and will continue to exist. Managing that divergence while maintaining the integrity of the UK is the challenge we face. It requires flexibility and creativity, not rigid insistence on uniformity where uniformity is not feasible.

People literally emptying savings, going into debt, making impossible choices between necessities. This is happening in one of the wealthiest countries in the world. It is a policy failure and a moral failure.

Energy bills have risen to levels that are simply unaffordable for many households. Food prices are climbing. Fuel costs are up. Wages for most people are not keeping pace. The result is a severe squeeze on living standards, particularly for those on low and fixed incomes.

The government's response has been inadequate. Small gestures and targeted measures help some people, but they do not address the scale of the crisis. We need comprehensive action to support households through this period and to address the underlying causes of inflation.

On energy specifically, we should be doing more to insulate homes and reduce energy consumption. That would lower bills and reduce carbon emissions. It is investment that pays for itself over time. Yet progress has been painfully slow.

On food prices, we need to look at competition in the grocery sector and at the power relationships in supply chains. Farmers are not benefiting from higher prices. The increase is being captured by intermediaries. Consumers are paying more while producers struggle. while producers are squeezed from both ends. That is not a functioning market. It is a sign of market power being exercised by large retailers and intermediaries.

We need a comprehensive cost-of-living strategy that addresses energy, food, housing, transport. Targeted measures help but they are not enough. We need systemic solutions that address the underlying causes of the crisis.

People cannot wait. They are suffering now. The Government needs to act with the urgency this situation demands.

GDP is increasing, so our contribution would increase on that basis alone. But we have also indicated willingness to contribute more from our own resources, above and beyond what the formula would require. That is a demonstration of our commitment.

The question the Deputy asked twice perhaps reflects some scepticism about this commitment. I want to be clear: this is not an empty promise. We have the fiscal capacity to contribute more. We recognise our responsibility as a relatively wealthy member state. We understand that solidarity is not just a rhetorical commitment.

There are ongoing discussions about the overall EU budget and about specific funding mechanisms. These are complex negotiations involving all member states. We cannot unilaterally decide what the final numbers will be. But we can and have signalled our willingness to be constructive.

I would also note that Ireland's contributions to the EU should be seen in context. We have benefited enormously from membership. The structural funds we received in earlier decades helped transform our economy. The single market has been hugely beneficial to Irish businesses. We have a strong interest in ensuring the EU is well funded and functional.

That is not just about money. It is about the kind of Europe we want to be part of. The context matters. Ireland has benefited enormously from EU membership over decades. We have received far more in structural funds than we contributed. We built our economy on access to the single market. We have a strong national interest in a well-functioning, well-funded EU.

So yes, we are willing to contribute more, and we are doing so from a position of understanding that it serves our interests as well as being the right thing to do.

The pattern we have seen over the years is fiscal irresponsibility dressed up as compassion. Promises are made without regard for how they will be paid for. Spending commitments are announced to win votes, with no sustainable plan for funding them. Taxes are increased on those who are productive to fund programmes that often do not achieve their stated goals.

In 2015, we inherited a balanced budget. That was the result of difficult decisions and fiscal discipline. It was not easy or popular, but it was necessary and responsible. It meant that Canada was in a strong position to respond to economic challenges.

What has happened since? The government has run deficits every year. They promised small, temporary deficits for infrastructure investment. Instead we have gotten large, ongoing deficits for operating expenses. The debt has grown substantially. Interest payments consume billions that could be spent on services.

When COVID hit, we needed fiscal capacity to respond. The fact that we had borrowed heavily during good economic times meant we were in a weaker position than we should have been. Other countries that had maintained fiscal discipline had more room to manoeuvre.

Now, with inflation rising and economic uncertainty growing, we are seeing the consequences of that fiscal irresponsibility. Now we are paying the price for that fiscal irresponsibility in the form of higher inflation, slower growth, and reduced capacity to respond to future challenges. This is the inevitable consequence of the pattern this government has followed, and Canadians deserve better.

Responsible fiscal management is not exciting. It does not win headlines. But it is essential for long-term prosperity and for having the resources available when they are genuinely needed.

I welcome the Minister's affordable housing scheme sincerely. It represents a recognition that the current market is failing low and middle income earners. People who work full time, who contribute to their communities, who do everything right, simply cannot afford to buy a home. That is not sustainable economically or socially.

What the Minister said in the Dáil last week gave me encouragement. It suggested that the scheme is being designed with genuine affordability in mind, not just marginal improvements that leave housing out of reach for most people. If this is done properly, it could be transformative.

But I have some questions and concerns that I hope the Minister can address. First, scale. How many homes are we actually talking about? If it is a few hundred or even a few thousand, that is helpful for those individuals but does not address the systemic problem. We need to be thinking in terms of tens of thousands of units.

Second, location. Affordable homes need to be where people actually want and need to live. That means proximity to jobs, schools, transport, services. Too often, affordable housing gets built in peripheral locations that require long commutes and lack amenities. The scheme needs to be delivered quickly. People cannot wait years for affordable housing. They need it now. So while I welcome the announcement, I will be watching closely to see whether it translates into actual homes that actual people can actually afford in reasonable timeframes and desirable locations.

If it does, this could be transformative. If it becomes another under-delivered promise, it will breed even more cynicism about whether government can solve this crisis.

This offence remains in the implementation. The approach to enforcement is consistent regardless of whether the maintenance decision was made domestically or by a foreign court. That consistency is important for clarity and for international cooperation.

The Lords amendment would have disrupted that consistency. It would have created different enforcement mechanisms depending on the origin of the decision. That would have been confusing for those administering the system and potentially problematic from an international law perspective.

I understand the concerns that motivated the Lords amendment. There are always questions about how enforcement powers will be used and whether they are proportionate. Those are legitimate questions that deserve serious consideration.

But the offence as included in the Bill already has safeguards. It requires demonstration that the failure to pay is willful and without reasonable excuse. It is not a strict liability offence. Courts will have discretion in sentencing. The enforcement mechanisms are appropriate to the seriousness of the issue.

Child maintenance is not a trivial matter. When one parent fails to pay, the other parent and the children suffer. Often, the parent owed maintenance is struggling financially precisely because they are the primary carer. I understand the goal of consistency and I appreciate the importance of international cooperation on enforcement. But I would urge continued attention to how these powers are used in practice and to whether safeguards are adequate.

The fundamental principle should be that children's welfare comes first and that parents who can pay maintenance should do so. How we enforce that principle matters, but the principle itself is not in doubt.

Many of the issues raised are already being addressed through our Programme for Government commitments, through our national policies and strategies, and through HSE service plans. We have made mental health a priority. We have committed additional funding. We have expanded services.

For older people specifically, there are initiatives to improve mental health supports, to combat social isolation, to ensure that services are age-appropriate and accessible. The HSE is working with voluntary organisations and community groups to deliver these services.

But I want to be realistic about the scale of the challenge. Mental health in older people is often overlooked. There is a tendency to assume that depression and anxiety are normal parts of aging, which they are not. There is stigma that prevents older people from seeking help. There are access barriers.

Loneliness and social isolation are major risk factors for mental health problems in older people. The pandemic has made this worse. People who previously had regular social contact through community groups, religious services, family visits, have been isolated for months. That takes a toll.

We need comprehensive approaches that address both mental health treatment and the social determinants of mental wellbeing. That means not just clinical services but also community supports, volunteer programmes, technology to help people stay connected. We cannot just expand clinical services. We need to address loneliness, social connection, purpose, community engagement. Those are not medical issues primarily. They are social issues that require social solutions.

I appreciate the work that is being done and the commitments that have been made. What I want to ensure is that older people's mental health gets the sustained attention and resources it deserves.

I cannot claim to be a natural gym enthusiast myself. My experiences with organized athletics in childhood were not entirely positive, and I have never quite recovered my enthusiasm for that particular form of recreation.

However, I fully recognise that for many people, gyms and fitness facilities are enormously important. They are places to improve health, to manage stress, to socialise, to build confidence. The pandemic closures were difficult for people who relied on gyms as part of their routine and wellbeing.

As we emerge from restrictions, we need to think carefully about how fitness and recreation facilities can operate safely. Ventilation is critical. Hygiene protocols need to be maintained. Capacity may need to be limited. But the goal should be getting these facilities open and accessible.

There is also a broader question about public health and physical activity. We know that sedentary lifestyles contribute to numerous health problems. We know that exercise improves both physical and mental health. Yet access to facilities is often limited by cost or location.

Some people can afford private gym memberships or have facilities through their workplace. Others do not have those options. That creates health inequalities that we should be addressing through public provision. access to sports facilities and recreation is a public good that government should provide, not a private commodity available only to those who can pay.

We should be thinking about how to make physical activity accessible to everyone regardless of income. That might mean more public leisure centres. It might mean subsidised memberships for low-income households. It might mean community sports programmes and outdoor facilities.

Investment in physical activity pays for itself many times over through reduced healthcare costs and improved population health. It is one of the best investments we can make.

The practice is wholly discriminatory and it places an unfair burden on people who cannot afford to buy new cars. We need to be honest about the fact that environmental and safety regulations, however well-intentioned, can have regressive effects if they are not designed carefully.

A ten-year-old car that has a valid NCT has met the required safety standards. It has been inspected and deemed roadworthy. Yet insurers are refusing to cover these vehicles, effectively forcing people to buy newer cars that they may not be able to afford.

For people on low incomes, this is a serious problem. They may have saved for years to buy a modest vehicle. They maintain it properly. They drive safely. Yet they are being told they cannot get insurance, or the premiums are so high that they are effectively priced out of driving.

In rural areas especially, this is not just an inconvenience. It affects people's ability to get to work, to access healthcare, to participate in community life. We cannot simply tell people to use public transport when public transport does not exist or does not serve their needs.

There are scrappage schemes and incentives for buying new cars. Those are helpful for some people. For those people, the choice is effectively between buying a new car they cannot afford or giving up driving altogether. That is not acceptable. We need regulation that protects consumers from discrimination while still allowing insurers to price risk appropriately.

Ten-year-old cars with valid NCTs should be insurable at reasonable rates. If they are not safe, they should not pass the NCT. But if they pass, they should be insurable. The current situation is unjust.

The Aga Khan Foundation is the organisation at the centre of this finding. The Prime Minister's relationship with the Aga Khan is personal and longstanding, which is precisely why he should have been scrupulous about avoiding any appearance of conflict.

Section 21 of the Conflict of Interest Act requires public office holders to recuse themselves from discussions where they could be in a position to further their own private interests or those of family or friends. This is not an obscure technicality. It is a fundamental principle of ethical government.

The Ethics Commissioner found that the Prime Minister contravened this section not once but twice. He participated in discussions where he had an opportunity to improperly further the private interests of someone with whom he has a close personal relationship. That is unacceptable.

The Prime Minister has said that the allegations were never brought to his attention. But the findings show that he was in a position where he should have been aware of the potential conflict. It is not sufficient to claim ignorance of your own conflicts of interest. You have a duty to be aware of them and to act accordingly.

Those in positions of authority have a duty to act on allegations and to avoid conflicts. The Prime Minister's failure to recuse himself from discussions where the Aga Khan Foundation's interests were at issue is exactly the kind of conflict the Act is designed to prevent. This is not a partisan issue. This is about basic standards of conduct that should apply to everyone regardless of party.

The House has called upon the Prime Minister to take action. I support that call and I believe it is the only appropriate response to the Ethics Commissioner's findings.

The commission's report makes clear that there were other actors involved in what happened in mother and baby homes. Religious orders ran many of these institutions, but they did so with state funding and state oversight. Local authorities placed women and children there. Families and communities shunned unmarried mothers and pressured them into the homes.

We cannot allow the religious orders to simply exit stage left and avoid responsibility. They were central players. They controlled the institutions. They made decisions about how women and children were treated. They hold records that are essential for understanding what happened.

But equally, we cannot let the state off the hook by focusing solely on the religious orders. The state funded these places. The state created the legal and policy framework that allowed them to operate. The state knew, or should have known, what conditions were like.

The challenge now is ensuring accountability from all responsible parties. That means financial redress where appropriate. It means access to records. It means acknowledgment of wrongdoing. It means reforms to prevent anything like this from happening again.

What we cannot have is a situation where everyone points fingers at everyone else while victims remain without justice or answers. We cannot allow collective responsibility to be dissolved into individual finger-pointing where no one is actually held accountable. The commission's report provides a roadmap. Now we need to follow it with concrete action: redress, access to records, accountability from all parties involved.

Anything less would be a betrayal of the women and children who suffered in these institutions.

The businesses and banks that are affected are in an extremely difficult position. Under European law and British law, their trade and investment with Iran is completely legal. They are not violating any domestic regulations. Yet under American law, they face the threat of severe sanctions.

This creates an impossible situation. Comply with one legal system and you violate another. The extraterritorial reach of American sanctions effectively forces companies to choose between doing business with Iran or doing business with the United States.
