Given the size and importance of the American market, that is not really a choice.

The government needs to be much more active in supporting our businesses and pushing back against American overreach. We have sovereignty. We have the right to determine our own foreign policy and our own trading relationships. We should not simply accept that American law governs what British companies can do.

This is not about supporting Iran's regime, which I certainly do not. It is about defending the principle that international trade should be governed by international law and by agreements like the Iran nuclear deal, which the United States has unilaterally withdrawn from but which European parties still support.

We need to work with our European partners to create mechanisms that allow legitimate trade to continue. What we need from our government is leadership on this issue. We need to work with European partners to develop mechanisms that protect legitimate business from extraterritorial overreach. We need to defend international law and multilateral agreements against unilateral American actions.

This is not about Iran specifically. It is about whether international trade is governed by law or by American diktat. That principle matters for our sovereignty and for a rules-based international order.

I appreciate the opportunity to ask a question. I have been listening carefully to the debate throughout the day. The issue before us is significant and the discussion has been valuable.

It is challenging when the speaking rounds are limited to ten minutes and five minutes. That does not allow for the kind of detailed engagement with complex issues that they deserve. I understand the need to give multiple members an opportunity to participate, but there is a tradeoff between breadth and depth.

My colleague from Longueuil-Charles-LeMoyne has made important points about the issues at stake. I want to build on those points and perhaps probe a bit deeper into some of the implications.

The question I want to raise concerns implementation. We can debate principles and we can debate policy. But ultimately what matters is how things work in practice for real people dealing with real situations. Too often, well-intentioned legislation creates problems in implementation that were not anticipated.

Have the proponents of this measure thought through the operational details? Have they consulted with those who would be responsible for administering it? Have they considered edge cases and unintended consequences? These are practical questions that need practical answers. My colleague has thoughtfully addressed many aspects of the issue. I want to build on those points and perhaps explore some additional dimensions that deserve consideration.

The practical implementation matters as much as the policy intent. We need to ensure that what sounds good in principle actually works in practice for the people it is meant to serve.

There is a clear obligation on employers to distribute tips fairly and transparently. Workers have a right to expect that gratuities left by customers will actually reach them. The WRC provides a mechanism for workers to seek redress if that is not happening.

Crucially, the system needs to be accessible and effective. If workers are afraid to complain because they fear retaliation, the right to redress is meaningless. If the WRC process is slow or cumbersome, workers will not use it. If penalties for violations are minimal, employers will not take the obligations seriously.

What concerns me is the gap between the formal rights that exist on paper and the practical ability of workers to enforce those rights. Hospitality workers are often young, vulnerable, working on precarious contracts. They may not know their rights. They may fear that complaining will cost them their job.

We need strong enforcement, proactive inspections, and meaningful penalties for employers who violate the rules. We also need better education so workers know what they are entitled to and how to assert their rights.

The broader issue is the casualisation and precarity in the hospitality sector. in the hospitality sector creates vulnerability. When workers do not have secure contracts, when they can be dismissed without cause, when they are dependent on tips to make a living wage, they are less likely to assert their rights even when they are being violated.

We need broader reforms to employment law that give workers more security and more power. That would make it easier for them to enforce rights including rights to fair distribution of tips. Strong individual rights are not enough without structural power to enforce them.

The Chancellor has created a system that provides support only to certain businesses in certain circumstances. If you are not in a Tier 3 area, no support. If you are in a Tier 3 area but choose to close because it is not safe to remain open, no support. If your business is devastated by restrictions but not legally required to close, no support.

This is not a safety net. A safety net catches everyone who falls. This is a system of narrow, targeted support that leaves large numbers of businesses without help precisely when they need it most.

Businesses that choose to close are making that choice for legitimate reasons. They cannot operate profitably under the restrictions. They are concerned about the safety of staff and customers. They are trying to get ahead of an inevitable forced closure. These are responsible decisions, and they should not be penalised.

The economic impact of these restrictions is not limited to businesses that are legally closed. Every business in a restricted area is affected. Footfall drops. Consumer spending falls. Supply chains are disrupted. The entire local economy contracts.

If the government is serious about supporting businesses through this crisis, the support needs to be broader and more flexible. Support that only catches some people who fall is not a safety net. It is a selection mechanism that leaves many without help.

The government needs to broaden eligibility, increase the level of support, and extend the duration. This crisis is not over. Businesses will continue to need help for months. Providing adequate support now is far cheaper than dealing with the consequences of mass business failures and unemployment later.

On top of the wreckage issue, the Department has compounded the problem by transferring responsibility to Cork County Council. The council is not equipped for marine salvage operations. They do not have the expertise, the equipment, or the resources for this kind of work.

This appears to be an attempt to pass the buck and avoid taking responsibility for a problem that clearly falls within the Department's remit. A shipwreck is not a local roads issue or a planning matter. It is a marine safety and environmental issue that requires specialist knowledge.

The people of Ballycotton have been raising this issue for months. They have contacted the Department multiple times. They have explained the safety hazards and the environmental concerns. They have been given vague assurances but no concrete action.

Meanwhile, the wreckage sits there, a hazard to navigation, a potential source of pollution, and an eyesore for a community that depends on tourism and fishing. Every day that passes without action is another day of risk.

What I want from the Minister is a clear explanation of why the Department has not dealt with this. Is it a question of funding? Is it a question of legal responsibility? The Department has clear responsibility for maritime safety and environmental protection. This wreckage falls squarely within that remit. Passing responsibility to Cork County Council is inappropriate and it looks like an attempt to avoid dealing with a difficult problem.

I want a clear answer about what the Department will do, and I want a timeline for getting it done. The people of Ballycotton have waited long enough.

I thank the Minister of State for that clarification. Carlow has quite a proud history with the Tidy Towns competition. Our communities take enormous pride in their appearance and in creating welcoming environments for residents and visitors alike.

Clonegal's national win two years ago was a tremendous achievement. It reflected years of dedicated work by volunteers who plant flowers, pick up litter, maintain public spaces, and organise community events. These are people who give their time freely because they love their village and want it to be the best it can be.

My own village has also won the award on three occasions. Each time, it was the result of the entire community coming together. Young and old, businesses and residents, all contributing to the effort. That is what makes Tidy Towns special. It is not just about how a place looks. It is about community spirit and pride.

What I want to emphasise is that this competition and the work it inspires is valuable beyond the awards themselves. Clean, well-maintained public spaces improve quality of life. They create civic pride. They make places more attractive for businesses and tourists. They demonstrate that people care about their community.

The government should continue to support Tidy Towns and similar initiatives. and recognise the dedication of volunteers who make Tidy Towns possible. Their work creates value that extends far beyond the competition itself. They are building community, creating pride, making places better to live.

That is work we should celebrate and support through adequate funding and through recognition like the Minister has provided today.

I would say that ranking Leaders of the Opposition is perhaps not the most productive use of our time. What matters is whether the opposition is holding the government to account effectively and proposing credible alternatives.

I have been in this House long enough to see several Leaders of the Opposition come and go. Some have been more effective than others. Some have gone on to become Prime Minister. Others have not. But I try to judge them on their arguments rather than on their party affiliation.

The shadow Minister's point, if I understood it correctly, was about consistency and principle. That is fair. We should all be consistent in our positions and principled in our approach to policy. We should not change our views simply because we move from opposition to government or vice versa.

But I would gently suggest that some degree of evolution is acceptable and even desirable. We learn from experience. Evidence accumulates. Circumstances change. It is not a sign of weakness to adjust one's position in light of new information.

What is not acceptable is rank opportunism, where positions are adopted purely for political advantage with no regard for consistency or principle. I like to think that all members of this House, whatever our disagreements, are trying to do what we believe is right. What is acceptable is being clear about what we believe and why we believe it while respecting that others may reach different conclusions. What is acceptable is evolving our views based on evidence and experience while maintaining core principles.

I try to approach politics in that spirit, and I believe most members of this House, across parties, do the same.

The Irish role in the United Nations has been one of our great contributions to the international community. We have consistently punched above our weight. Our peacekeepers are respected around the world. Our diplomats have been effective advocates for human rights, for development, for multilateralism.

This is a source of pride and it is central to our national identity. We are a small country, but we have chosen to be active and engaged in global affairs. We have aligned ourselves with international law and with the principles of the UN Charter.

Some voices in this House would prefer a more narrow focus on immediate national interests. They question the value of our international commitments. They would have us withdraw from engagement with global challenges that do not directly affect us.

I reject that view. Ireland's interests are served by a stable, law-governed international order. We are too small to impose our will on others, so we benefit from a system where might does not make right. We depend on international trade and cooperation. We need allies and partners.

Our peacekeeping contributions are not charity. They are an investment in the kind of world we want to live in. They give us credibility and influence. and with the peacekeeping and humanitarian work we do through the UN. We have built a reputation as honest brokers, as committed to international law, as reliable partners. That is valuable and we should be proud of it.

Some would have us withdraw, turn inward, focus narrowly on immediate material interests. I believe that would diminish us and ultimately harm our interests. We are better served by engagement than by isolation.

In 2017, we brought forward our first legislation on quads and scramblers. These vehicles have been a plague on communities for years. Illegal use, dangerous driving, noise, antisocial behaviour. Residents living in fear. Children at risk. Gardaí unable to pursue because of safety concerns.

We put forward a comprehensive Bill to tackle this problem. We proposed measures to regulate ownership, to require registration, to give Gardaí enforcement powers. It was debated in 2018 and it was voted down. The Government at the time said it was not necessary or would not work.

Since then, the problem has only gotten worse. More incidents. More injuries. More communities affected. And now, finally, the Government has recognised that legislation is needed. They are bringing forward their own Bill, which in many respects mirrors what we proposed years ago.

I do not say this to claim credit or to score political points. What I want to highlight is the cost of delay. If this had been addressed in 2018, how many incidents could have been prevented? How many people would have been spared injury or trauma? How many communities would have been spared years of disruption?

This is a pattern we see too often. When Sinn Féin finally proposed legislation, we should have listened. We should have worked together to refine it and pass it. Instead, it was voted down and years were lost. Now we are finally addressing the problem, but the cost of that delay has been substantial.

I hope we can learn from this and be more willing to work across party lines on issues that affect communities regardless of politics.

I worked in the North Sea for BP. I worked in that industry for 25 years. I know it intimately. I know the people who work in it. I know the communities that depend on it. And I know the challenges it faces.

So when I hear debates about the future of oil and gas, I bring that experience and perspective. This is not abstract for me. It is about people I worked alongside, about communities I am part of, about an industry that has contributed enormously to our economy and our energy security.

We need to be realistic about the energy transition. It will not happen overnight. We will continue to need oil and gas for decades, even as we scale up renewables. The question is where that oil and gas comes from and how it is produced.

Domestic production can be done to high environmental standards with proper regulation and oversight. It provides jobs and tax revenue. It reduces our dependence on imports from countries with lower standards and questionable regimes.

At the same time, we need to be investing heavily in renewable energy, in energy efficiency, in the technologies that will power the future. The oil and gas industry can and should be part of that transition. The skills and expertise developed in offshore oil and gas are directly applicable to offshore wind. What I bring to debates about energy policy is not ideology but experience. I know what is possible and what is not. I know the economics and the engineering. I know the people whose livelihoods depend on getting this right.

We need to transition away from fossil fuels. That is clear. But we need to do it in a way that is realistic, that maintains energy security, that protects workers and communities. That requires listening to people who actually know the industry, not just to those with strong opinions but limited understanding.

We heard testimony from survivors who experienced horrific abuse in residential schools. Physical abuse, sexual abuse, psychological abuse. Children taken from their families and communities. Languages and cultures suppressed. Generations traumatised.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented all of this. The calls to action provide a roadmap for moving forward. But we need to be honest about how much work remains to be done and how much resistance there is to actually implementing those calls.

Reconciliation is not just a matter of apologies and symbolic gestures. It requires concrete action. It requires returning land. It requires providing resources for healing and rebuilding. It requires changing laws and policies that continue to discriminate against indigenous peoples. It requires addressing the ongoing issues like the water crisis, the housing crisis, the disproportionate incarceration rates.

And it requires listening. Truly listening, not just performatively consulting. Indigenous peoples have been telling us what they need and what they want. We need to centre their voices and follow their lead.

What I am hearing in some of the comments today is a reluctance to actually do the difficult work that reconciliation requires. There is an eagerness to move past the uncomfortable truths, to declare the matter settled, to avoid the structural changes that are necessary. The work of reconciliation is difficult and it will take generations. But we have to do it. We have to confront the truth. We have to listen to indigenous voices. We have to make structural changes that redistribute power and resources.

Anything less is a continuation of colonialism by other means. Anything less fails to honour the survivors and the victims. Anything less leaves the fundamental problems unaddressed.

The fund represents a real opportunity to invest in infrastructure that has been neglected for too long. Our town centres and high streets have been struggling. Local transport is inadequate in many areas. This is a chance to reverse decades of underinvestment and to build the foundations for genuine levelling up.

Regenerating town centres is about more than just physical infrastructure. It is about creating places where people want to live and work and spend time. That means good public spaces, cultural facilities, local shops and services. It means addressing empty buildings and derelict sites. It means making places safe and attractive.

Local transport is critical for connecting communities and enabling people to access opportunities. Too many people are trapped in car dependency because there is no viable alternative. Buses are infrequent and expensive. Cycling infrastructure is dangerous or non-existent. Walking routes are poorly maintained.

Investment in these areas will create jobs during construction and ongoing economic benefits once completed. Better town centres attract businesses and visitors. Better transport enables people to get to work and to access services. These are the kinds of investments that pay for themselves many times over.

The challenge will be ensuring that funding is distributed fairly and that projects are chosen on merit. The challenge is political. There are vested interests that benefit from the status quo. There are ideological commitments to private provision regardless of outcomes. There is reluctance to invest the resources required for transformation.

But the benefits would be enormous. Better connected communities, reduced carbon emissions, improved productivity, enhanced quality of life. These are the foundations of levelling up, if we are serious about it.

Not bad for a four-year-old, indeed. My daughter has had the opportunity to visit Parliament Hill on numerous occasions, and each time she comes away inspired by the work that happens here and by the possibilities of public service.

She has dressed as a parliamentary page, absorbing the formality and tradition of this place. She has dressed as the Speaker, understanding the role of presiding over our debates with fairness and authority. Most recently, she came dressed as a commercial-rated pilot, which reflects her current fascination with aviation.

What strikes me about these visits is her curiosity and her ambition. She asks questions about how things work, about why we do things certain ways, about what is possible. She does not see barriers or limitations. She sees opportunities.

That is what we should want for all children. We should want them to believe that they can be anything, do anything, contribute to society in whatever way calls to them. We should want them to see institutions like Parliament not as remote or irrelevant but as places where important work happens and where they could someday play a role.

I am grateful that my daughter has had these experiences. I am aware that not all children have the same opportunities. I want all children to have opportunities to see how our democracy works and to imagine themselves as part of it. I want them to believe they can shape their future and their community. My daughter has had that advantage. Every child should.

That is one reason I do this work. Not just for my own children, but for all children. Building a society where opportunity is broadly shared, where potential is not wasted, where everyone can contribute their talents.

She has been a tireless advocate for Syria from the very beginning of the conflict. When others have moved on to the next crisis, when Syria has faded from the headlines, she has kept speaking out. She has kept the issue in front of Parliament and in the public consciousness.

That consistency and persistence matters enormously. It is easy to speak out when something is in the news and everyone is paying attention. It is much harder to keep going year after year when attention has moved elsewhere but the suffering continues.

The hon. Lady has travelled to the region. She has met with refugees and with aid workers. She has visited camps. She has heard firsthand testimony about conditions and about needs. That direct engagement gives her advocacy credibility and moral force.

She has also worked across party lines, building coalitions and finding common ground. She understands that Syria is not a partisan issue. It is a humanitarian catastrophe that demands a response that transcends political divisions.

The people of Syria will not be forgotten as long as she is in this House, and we are all better for her presence and her advocacy. She sets an example of what effective parliamentary work looks like. She identifies an issue, she studies it carefully, she speaks out persistently, she works with others to advance solutions. The people of Syria will not be forgotten as long as the hon. Lady is in this House speaking for them. Her advocacy sets an example for all of us about what effective parliamentary work looks like and what it can achieve.

I commend her for her dedication and I pledge to support her efforts to keep Syria on our agenda and to push for meaningful action to address the ongoing crisis.

The combined authority is taking the commission's recommendations seriously and undertaking a comprehensive review of its local transport plan. That review is focused on the areas that matter most: active travel and low carbon solutions.

Active travel means walking and cycling, which are healthiest and most sustainable forms of transport for short journeys. We need infrastructure that makes these options safe and attractive. That means protected cycle lanes, not just painted lines on roads. It means wide, well-maintained pavements. It means crossing points that prioritise pedestrians.

Low carbon solutions for longer journeys mean electric buses, trams, light rail. We need to shift people out of private cars and onto public transport. That requires service that is frequent, reliable, affordable, and comprehensive enough to actually serve people's needs.

The bus reform proposals are particularly important. The current deregulated system has failed passengers. Routes are designed for commercial profitability rather than public need. Timetables are not coordinated. Fares are confusing and expensive. Bringing services under public control would allow us to design a network that actually works for people.

As a former shadow Transport Minister, I have studied how other cities and regions have approached these challenges. best practices from elsewhere and applied them to our context. That expertise and experience should inform our approach here.

The review represents an opportunity to get this right. We should not waste it through timidity or by privileging commercial interests over public need. We should be bold in our vision and thorough in our implementation.

This law is necessary because time is working against us. The generation that witnessed the Holocaust is passing away. In another decade or two, there will be no survivors left to tell their stories from personal experience. The events will be entirely historical, known only through documents and recorded testimony.

As that happens, as the immediacy fades, there is a risk that denial and distortion will become more widespread. Already we see troubling trends in surveys of young people, showing ignorance about basic historical facts. We see conspiracy theories spreading online. We see extremist movements attempting to rehabilitate fascism.

This law is a firewall against that. It establishes that there are limits to acceptable discourse. It protects the memory of the victims. It honours the survivors. It sends a clear message about our values as a society.

Some worry about free speech implications. I share those concerns in general. But Holocaust denial is not an exercise in free inquiry or historical debate. It is a form of propaganda designed to rehabilitate an evil ideology. Other democracies have laws against it without becoming authoritarian states.

The law will help us avoid the mainstreaming and creeping into popular culture of ideas that should be beyond the pale. As Holocaust memory becomes entirely historical rather than living, we need mechanisms to preserve it and to transmit it to new generations. This law is one such mechanism. It establishes that certain lies will not be tolerated, that memory will be protected.

That is not an assault on free speech. It is a defence of truth and a commitment to never again allowing the conditions that led to genocide.

Prince Philip's service to this country spanned seven decades. That is an almost incomprehensible length of time to dedicate to public duty. Through all the changes our country has experienced, through wars and social transformations, through technological revolutions, he was a constant presence supporting the Queen and representing the nation.

For the people of Penrith and The Border, his connection to our region was meaningful. He visited on numerous occasions. He engaged with local organisations. He understood rural communities and the challenges they face. He was a genuine supporter of farming, of land management, of rural enterprises.

His dedication to public service was humbling. He could have lived a life of leisure and privilege. Instead, he chose to work, to engage, to contribute. He undertook thousands of engagements, often in the background, without fanfare or recognition. He simply got on with the job.

That kind of dedication is increasingly rare in our culture. We live in an age of celebrity and self-promotion, where people seek attention and accolades for minimal effort. Prince Philip represented something different: quiet, consistent service without expectation of personal glory.

His legacy will endure through the organisations he founded and supported. through the Duke of Edinburgh Award and his other initiatives. Millions of lives improved. Confidence built. Opportunities created. That legacy will endure.

We honour his memory best by continuing the work he championed and by embodying the values of service and dedication he exemplified throughout his remarkable life.

I think we are seeing a necessary reality check across the country and in this House. There was a period of optimism and perhaps unrealistic expectations about how quickly we could emerge from restrictions and return to normal. Now we are confronting the actual complexity and difficulty of the situation.

The realism from the Government yesterday was welcome. They acknowledged challenges. They outlined a careful, phased approach. They showed awareness of the risks of moving too quickly. That is the right approach, even though it is not what people want to hear.

Progress in several areas has been good. Vaccination is proceeding. Case numbers have come down from the peaks. Health services have coped better than was feared. These are genuine achievements that should be acknowledged.

But we also need a reality check about what happens next. This is not over. The virus is still circulating. New variants are emerging. The path out of this will be gradual and uncertain. There will be setbacks and adjustments.

Economically, the recovery will take time. Some jobs will not come back. Some businesses will not survive. Some sectors will be permanently changed. We need support that recognises that reality rather than assuming a quick bounce back to pre-pandemic conditions. There was realism yesterday that was welcome and necessary. We are confronting the actual difficulty of the situation rather than clinging to optimistic projections that are not grounded in reality.

Progress has been made and should be acknowledged. But we need to be honest about the challenges ahead and realistic about timelines for recovery. That honesty is the foundation for effective policy.

The strength of our report is precisely its practicality and feasibility. We have not proposed some grand, expensive, long-term scheme that might never be delivered. We have identified concrete measures that can be implemented in a reasonable timeframe with manageable costs.

Business rates are a perfect example. Seventy-five percent of business rates go to local government. That is substantial revenue that councils depend on for services. But the system is outdated and in many cases unfair. It penalises physical retail at a time when high streets are struggling. It does not adequately capture the value generated by digital businesses.

Reform is overdue and it is doable. We have laid out specific options. We have modelled the fiscal impacts. We have consulted with businesses and with local authorities. This is not pie in the sky. It is a worked-out proposal that could be implemented if there is political will.

What we need now is for the government to take our recommendations seriously and act on them. Too often, parliamentary reports are published, there is a brief flurry of attention, and then they gather dust. That would be a wasted opportunity.

The issues we have addressed are not going away. What we have identified are practical measures that can be implemented without enormous cost or endless delay. The government should act on our recommendations. Parliament has done its job. Now the executive needs to do theirs.

I have not heard those exact words, so I will not comment on a characterisation of something I did not witness. What I will say is that there has been extensive commentary about this Bill from many quarters, and we have listened carefully to all of it.

What is important is the reality of what the Bill does, not selective quotations or interpretations of commentary. The Bill provides certainty for Northern Irish businesses. It ensures unfettered access to the GB market. It implements the protocol in a way that minimises friction and disruption.

Northern Irish businesses have been clear about what they need. They need to know the rules. They need to be able to trade with Great Britain without barriers. They need support in dealing with any new requirements. This Bill delivers that.

There will always be different views on complex policy issues. That is the nature of democratic debate. Some people will focus on concerns and criticisms. Others will focus on benefits and opportunities. We have tried to strike a balance, listening to concerns while maintaining the essential elements.

The reality is that Northern Ireland has a unique position, with access to both the UK market and the EU single market. That creates opportunities as well as complexities. The reality is what the Bill actually does for Northern Irish businesses and for implementing the protocol in a workable way. That reality is what matters, not selective interpretations of commentary.

Northern Ireland has a unique opportunity to benefit from access to both markets. This Bill helps make that opportunity real.

This Bill is a step forward, but it does not address all the issues with electric vehicles. There is much more work to be done to create a comprehensive framework that supports the transition to electric transport.

The national grid of charging points is essential. People will not buy electric vehicles if they are worried about running out of charge. Range anxiety is real and it is a significant barrier to adoption. We need charging infrastructure that is ubiquitous, reliable, and fast.

That infrastructure needs to be planned strategically. Charging points need to be in convenient locations: motorway service areas, car parks, residential streets. There needs to be enough capacity to handle peak demand. And the grid itself needs to be upgraded to supply the electricity.

Interoperability is another crucial issue. Consumers should not need multiple apps and membership cards to access different charging networks. It should be as simple as filling up with petrol: pull up, charge, pay, leave. The current fragmented system is confusing and off-putting.

This Bill moves us in the right direction on some of these issues, but it is not comprehensive. We need a full national strategy on electric vehicle infrastructure, coordinated across government departments and with local authorities and private providers. We need that comprehensive strategy urgently. The transition to electric vehicles is happening. The question is whether we manage it well or allow it to happen chaotically with insufficient infrastructure and poor consumer experience.

This Bill is a step. We need many more steps to have a complete solution.

Ratification of the UN convention is long overdue. People with disabilities in this country face systemic discrimination in employment, education, transport, housing, healthcare. That discrimination is pervasive and it is unjust. Ratifying the convention is an important step, but it is only a step.

The convention establishes rights and sets standards. It provides a framework for assessing whether we are meeting our obligations to people with disabilities. It creates accountability mechanisms. These are valuable.

But rights on paper are meaningless without implementation. We can ratify the convention and then ignore it. We can produce nice statements about inclusion and equality while doing nothing to actually remove barriers and address discrimination.

What I want to see is concrete action. Accessible public transport, not just token efforts. Mainstream schools resourced to include children with disabilities, not segregated special education. Employment support that actually helps people with disabilities get and keep jobs. Housing that is designed for accessibility from the start, not adapted as an afterthought.

I commend my party colleagues who have campaigned persistently for ratification. They have kept this issue on the agenda and they have refused to accept delay and inaction. Concrete action is what will make the difference. Ratification is important. Implementation is essential. We need to judge ourselves not by the conventions we sign but by the outcomes we achieve for people with disabilities.

I will continue to press for that action and to hold the Government accountable for delivering on the commitments that ratification represents.

The petition addresses an issue that is critical for my constituents and for British Columbians generally: the crisis facing Pacific salmon. These fish are an icon of our region. They are central to indigenous cultures. They support commercial and recreational fisheries. They are a keystone species in our ecosystems.

And they are in serious trouble. Populations have crashed. Returns have been far below historical levels. Entire runs are at risk of extinction. This is an ecological catastrophe and it is happening on our watch.

The causes are multiple. Habitat destruction from development and logging. Climate change affecting water temperatures and ocean conditions. Pollution. Overfishing. And the impact of fish farms, which is one of the key concerns raised in the petition.

There is a fundamental conflict of interest when the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is responsible both for promoting the aquaculture industry and for protecting wild fish. Those mandates are not compatible. The fox is guarding the henhouse.

Petitioners are calling on the government to remove this conflict, to prioritise wild salmon, and to take urgent action to protect and restore populations. These are reasonable demands and they deserve a serious response. Petitioners are calling for action that would protect wild salmon and ensure their survival for future generations. That is a reasonable demand that deserves a serious response, not deflection or delay.

The government needs to act before it is too late.

We reduced excise duty by 15 cent per litre. That was a significant intervention in response to extraordinary price increases caused by the war in Ukraine and by global energy market disruptions. It has provided some relief to consumers and to businesses.

The diesel rebate for the haulage sector recognises that transport costs feed through into the cost of everything else. When hauliers are paying more for fuel, those costs are passed on. Food costs more. Building materials cost more. Everything costs more. Supporting the haulage sector helps moderate inflation across the economy.

But as Deputy Verona Murphy knows, these are temporary measures addressing an acute crisis. They are expensive in terms of lost revenue. They do not address the underlying need to transition away from fossil fuels. They are not sustainable as long-term policy.

What we need is a comprehensive approach to transport and energy that reduces our dependence on imported fossil fuels, invests in alternatives, and protects households and businesses from price volatility. That includes public transport, active travel, electric vehicles, renewable energy.

In the meantime, we are doing what we can to cushion the impact of current high prices. In the meantime, the measures we have taken provide meaningful relief. They show that we are responsive to genuine crisis and willing to act to help people. That is what government should do.

But temporary relief is not the same as long-term strategy. We need both.

The SNP has consistently called for tax avoidance and evasion powers to be devolved to Scotland. We believe we would do a better job of tackling these issues than Westminster has done. The track record speaks for itself: too many loopholes, too little enforcement, too much revenue lost.

We think we would do better on most things if they were devolved to Scotland, to be clear. That is the fundamental principle of devolution. Decisions should be made as close as possible to the people they affect. Scottish solutions for Scottish issues.

But on tax avoidance and evasion specifically, there are particular reasons to think devolution would be beneficial. We could tailor our approach to Scottish circumstances. We could be more responsive and more innovative. We could prioritise fairness and revenue collection rather than political considerations that dominate at Westminster.

Other countries manage tax policy at national and subnational levels. Federal systems exist and function well. There is no technical barrier to Scotland having greater tax powers. The barrier is political.

What we are asking for is not radical. It is the normal arrangement in many democracies. The barriers are political, not technical. Westminster guards its powers jealously. But devolution is supposed to be about trusting people to govern themselves. Scotland should have the tools it needs to tackle tax avoidance and evasion effectively.

We will continue to press for those powers to be devolved.

I want to particularly mention the excellent leadership of Cardiff City Council under Huw Thomas and his Welsh Labour colleagues. During the pandemic, they have demonstrated what effective local government can achieve when it is properly led and adequately resourced.

They acted quickly to set up support systems for vulnerable residents. They established advice lines. They coordinated with voluntary organisations and community groups. They made sure that no one in Cardiff needed to go hungry or to go without essential support.

That kind of practical, compassionate governance makes an enormous difference to people's lives. It is easy to talk about values and principles. It is harder to actually deliver services that help people in crisis. Cardiff Council has done that.

What strikes me is the contrast between local government's response to the pandemic and some of what we have seen from national government. Local authorities have been pragmatic, focused on meeting needs, willing to work across party lines. They have been accountable and responsive.

This is what government should look like. Not grandstanding or blame-shifting, but practical problem-solving focused on serving the public. Cardiff's example should be studied and learned from. This example should be studied and replicated. Effective local government during crisis shows what is possible when leadership is focused on serving people rather than on partisan advantage.

I commend Cardiff Council and I hope their approach inspires others.

I remember when my mother took me to the bank at age 16 to open my first account. That was an important rite of passage. It marked becoming financially independent, taking responsibility for my own money, entering the adult world in a small but significant way.

She gave me £20 to start the account, which was a considerable sum in those days. It represented sacrifice on her part and trust in me. I understood that I needed to be responsible, to save, to manage the account properly.

The paper trail of banking, as I mentioned, has value. There is something tangible about a passbook, about deposit slips, about cheques. You can see your money, track your spending, understand where you stand. It is not just numbers on a screen.

I worry sometimes that the move to entirely digital banking, while convenient, loses something important. Young people do not have that experience of going to the bank, interacting with staff, learning the systems. It is all apps and online platforms that can feel abstract.

There is also a question of financial inclusion. Not everyone has smartphones or reliable internet access. Not everyone is comfortable with technology. Digital-only banking can exclude vulnerable populations. The move to digital banking has benefits but it also has costs. We need to ensure that as we modernise financial services, we do not exclude or disadvantage vulnerable populations who depend on traditional banking services.

Financial inclusion needs to be a priority as we navigate the transition to digital systems.

I talked about gains repeatedly in relation to aluminum. I gave specific examples of how the agreement provides much stronger protection than what existed before. Seventy-five percent for the total vehicle, seventy-five percent for core products, seventy percent for aluminum purchased by manufacturers.

These are real, meaningful improvements. They will support aluminum production in Canada. They will protect jobs. They will ensure that our industry benefits from North American auto manufacturing rather than being undercut by imports.

The criticism I am hearing seems to be that we did not get everything we wanted. That is the nature of negotiation. You have competing interests. You have to compromise. The question is whether the outcome is better than the status quo and whether it is better than the alternatives.

On both counts, the answer is yes. This agreement is significantly better protection than existed before. And the alternative, if negotiations had failed, would have been harmful to Canadian interests.

I understand that there are some provisions that are not perfect. I am happy to discuss specific concerns. But the characterisation of this agreement as somehow weakening protections is simply wrong. The facts do not support that claim. The facts support the claim that this agreement provides stronger protection for Canadian aluminum. The specific percentages I cited demonstrate that. I am happy to defend the agreement on its merits because the merits are strong.

Criticism should be specific and factual. Vague claims that the agreement is somehow bad for Canada do not hold up to scrutiny.

I speak on behalf of my constituents in Luton South and those of my hon. Friend the Member for Luton North. The petition addresses the serious financial crisis facing Luton Council as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The petition declares that the crisis has placed extraordinary pressures on local government finances. Councils have faced surging costs for social care, for public health, for supporting vulnerable residents. At the same time, revenues have collapsed as businesses closed and economic activity contracted.

Luton has been particularly hard hit. The town's economy is heavily dependent on the airport and on related industries. When aviation shut down, Luton suffered disproportionately. Job losses, business failures, plummeting tax revenues.

The council has responded admirably, providing essential services and support despite the financial pressures. But they cannot continue indefinitely without adequate funding from central government. There are limits to what councils can do by cutting costs and using reserves.

What we need is a comprehensive support package that recognises the specific challenges Luton faces. Not just general funding formulae, but targeted help for areas that have been disproportionately affected by the pandemic and its economic fallout. Luton's specific circumstances demand targeted help. The government should provide it. Our constituents deserve no less.

I will continue to press for adequate support for Luton Council and for the communities they serve.

I welcome the Minister's statement that the bypass will not proceed in its entirety. That is a significant concession and it reflects the concerns that have been raised by the community and by myself and other public representatives.

However, I remain significantly concerned that some form of bypass is still planned. This is a troubling situation. The community has been clear in its opposition. The environmental arguments against the bypass are strong. The costs are substantial. Yet we are still proceeding.

What makes this particularly frustrating is how this decision has been made. On two occasions this year, the HSE has issued statements about the project that contradict each other or that have had to be clarified or walked back. That creates confusion and undermines trust.

If a decision has been made to proceed with a modified bypass, that should be explained clearly. What will it look like? What will it cost? What are the alternatives that were considered? Why is it necessary? These questions deserve clear answers, not vague assurances.

The community deserves to be properly consulted and to have their concerns addressed. This is their area. The bypass will affect them. The bypass project has been controversial from the start. The community has made its views clear. The Government should listen to those views and should be transparent about what is planned and why.

I will continue to represent my constituents' concerns on this issue and to press for clarity and proper consultation.

This is an important issue, but it is unfortunate that statements like this are often used as fillers at the end of the parliamentary day or scheduled at times when the chamber is not full and media attention is minimal.

If we are serious about an issue, we should schedule it for prime time when members are present and when it will receive appropriate scrutiny and coverage. Relegating it to the end of the day sends a message about its priority, regardless of what we say about its importance.

That said, I am grateful for the opportunity to address the issue at all. There are many important matters that never make it onto the agenda. So while the timing is not ideal, I will take advantage of the opportunity we have.

The substance of what we are discussing today matters enormously to affected communities and individuals. They deserve to have their concerns heard and addressed by this House. They deserve to see their elected representatives engaging seriously with the issues that affect their lives.

What I would urge is that in future, when we are scheduling statements and debates, we think carefully about what message we send through when and how we schedule them. If we treat important issues as afterthoughts by scheduling them poorly, we send a message about our priorities that undermines our rhetoric about caring.

We should match our scheduling to our stated values.

I spoke on this topic previously in October 2019 when I highlighted the Barnardo's report on child sexual exploitation. I want to return to that report now because the issues it raises have not gone away. If anything, they have become more urgent.

Barnardo's survey found that one third of children who are sexually exploited are looked-after children. That is a shocking statistic that demands our attention. These are children who are supposed to be in the care of the state, protected from harm. Yet they are disproportionately vulnerable to exploitation.

In 2018-19, Barnardo's helped 498 children who had been sexually exploited. Each one of those is a child who experienced abuse. Each one represents a failure of the systems that should have kept them safe.

We need to understand why looked-after children are so vulnerable. Part of it is the trauma and instability they have already experienced. Part of it is the disruption of placements and relationships. Part of it is inadequate support and supervision.

And we need to act on that understanding. Better training for social workers and foster carers to recognise signs of exploitation. More stable placements. More intensive support for children at risk. Looked-after children deserve better. They deserve to be safe. They deserve support to heal from trauma. They deserve to have their vulnerabilities recognised and addressed rather than exploited.

That requires investment and it requires system change. We cannot keep failing these children.

Rising inflation is already causing enormous pain for pensioners and will continue to do so. Pensioners on fixed incomes are particularly vulnerable to inflation because they cannot increase their income through work. When prices rise, their living standards fall.

The combination of increased food costs, energy price hikes, and the government's retrograde decision to scrap free TV licences for over-75s creates a perfect storm. Pensioners are being hit from multiple directions simultaneously.

Now we are facing an unprecedented rise in wholesale energy prices that will feed through into bills this winter. For pensioners who are already choosing between heating and eating, this could be catastrophic. We could see pensioners dying from cold because they cannot afford to heat their homes adequately.

The targeted help that has been announced is not enough. It helps some pensioners, but many will fall through the gaps. And even those who receive help will still face enormous financial pressure.

What we need is a comprehensive support package that recognises the specific vulnerabilities of pensioners. Higher state pension increases to match inflation. Energy price cap protections. Restoration of free TV licences. Support for insulation and energy efficiency improvements. The targeted help announced is not enough. Many pensioners will fall through gaps. The government needs to do more to protect pensioners from this unprecedented cost-of-living crisis.

Pensioners built this country. They deserve to live their later years in dignity and security, not in poverty and cold.

The year 2020 has been grim, there is no avoiding that reality. All of us have lost things this year. Time with loved ones. Celebrations and milestones. Freedoms we took for granted. For many, the losses have been far worse: jobs, businesses, health, family members.

Nobody wants these restrictions. They are not imposed out of malice or desire for control. They are necessary responses to a deadly virus that has killed hundreds of thousands of people and that threatens to overwhelm our health system if left unchecked.

I welcome the restrictions and I will vote with the Government this evening on all the motions. That is not because I am happy about them. It is because I accept that they are necessary and that the alternatives would be worse.

The retrospective nature of this legislation has raised concerns, and those concerns are legitimate. Parliament should authorise restrictions before they are imposed, not after. That is a principle that matters.

But we are living in exceptional circumstances. The virus does not wait for parliamentary schedules. Decisions have had to be made quickly in response to changing situations. I trust that this retrospective authorisation is an exception driven by necessity, not a precedent for normal times. We are living in exceptional times that require exceptional measures. The retrospective nature of this legislation is not ideal, but I accept it as necessary in the circumstances we face.

I will vote for the measures because they are necessary to protect public health, even though I wish the process had been different.

Thirty-nine percent of jobs in my constituency are in sectors that have been identified as severely impacted by a no-deal Brexit or a bad deal with the EU. That is not a theoretical concern or abstract modelling. It is people's livelihoods, families' security, communities' economic foundations.

I am extremely angry, as are my constituents, that as a Member of Parliament I will have very little say over what kind of relationship we have with the EU. We are being presented with a binary choice: accept whatever deal is negotiated or crash out with no deal. That is not meaningful parliamentary sovereignty.

We were promised that Brexit would restore parliamentary control. That Parliament would take back power from unelected bureaucrats in Brussels. Yet when it comes to the most important decision this Parliament will make in a generation, we are being sidelined.

I want to scrutinise the deal. I want to understand the trade-offs. I want to assess whether it serves my constituents' interests. I want the opportunity to propose amendments or alternatives. That is what parliamentary sovereignty should mean.

Instead, we are being presented with a fait accompli and told to vote for it or accept the chaos of no deal. Instead, we are being presented with whatever the government negotiates and told to take it or leave it. That is not taking back control. That is executive overreach.

I am angry about this and my constituents are angry. We deserve better.

That quote was from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, the member for Winnipeg North. The Liberals campaigned on a promise to improve retirement income security for all Canadian seniors. It is time they delivered on that promise.

Seniors built this country. They worked hard their entire lives. They paid taxes. They raised families. They contributed to their communities. They deserve to live their retirement years in dignity and security, not in poverty or financial stress.

Yet too many seniors are struggling. Pensions are inadequate. Savings have been eroded. The cost of living keeps rising. Many seniors are working well past retirement age not by choice but by necessity.

The government has made small improvements. The recent increase to Old Age Security for seniors over 75 was welcome. But it created a two-tier system where seniors aged 65 to 74 are left behind. All seniors face high costs of living. All seniors deserve adequate support.

We need comprehensive pension reform that ensures all seniors have enough to live on. That means higher payments across the board. It means indexing to inflation so that benefits do not lose value. It means addressing the gaps that leave some seniors particularly vulnerable. The government campaigned on improving retirement security. They need to deliver on that promise for all seniors, not just for some.

Seniors deserve dignity, security, and adequate support. That is not too much to ask from a government that promised to help them.

I am very grateful to the hon. Gentleman for putting that on the record. I appreciate his acknowledgment that Sinn Féin are not present to speak for themselves. I engage with them regularly, as he knows, and I will continue to do that.

The question of how we engage with parties who do not take their seats is always delicate. On one hand, they are elected representatives of significant constituencies. Their constituents' interests deserve to be represented. On the other hand, they have made a choice not to participate in this chamber.

I try to find ways to ensure that Northern Irish interests are heard and considered, regardless of which party represents them. That means engaging with Sinn Féin outside this chamber, consulting with community representatives, listening to voices from across Northern Ireland.

It is not a perfect solution. There is no substitute for direct parliamentary representation and debate. But given the reality of the situation, we have to find workable arrangements.

What I hope is that over time, Sinn Féin will reconsider their abstentionist position. This chamber is where laws affecting their constituents are made. Their constituents would be better served by their presence and participation. Sinn Féin's constituents deserve representation. I try to ensure their interests are considered even though their elected representatives are not present in this chamber.

It is an imperfect arrangement but it is the best we can do given the reality of abstentionism.

I would like to ask the government House leader for his explanation to Canadians as to why this Parliament cannot sit three days a week with reduced numbers, as we have seen functioning today and as was proposed by the opposition.

We are in extraordinary times. The pandemic has created unprecedented challenges. Canadians are looking to Parliament for leadership, for oversight, for accountability. Yet we are not sitting with anything approaching normal frequency.

The argument that it is not safe for Parliament to meet does not hold water. We have demonstrated today that we can meet safely with reduced numbers and appropriate health measures. Other legislatures around the world have found ways to continue functioning. We should be able to do the same.

The government seems to prefer making announcements to facing questions. They want to roll out programs and spend billions of dollars without parliamentary scrutiny. That is not how our system is supposed to work.

Parliament exists to hold the government to account, to scrutinise spending, to represent constituents' concerns. We cannot do that if we are not sitting. Virtual participation helps but it is not a substitute for Parliament functioning properly. Canadians deserve a functioning Parliament that provides oversight and accountability. We can meet safely. We should meet regularly. The government should welcome scrutiny rather than avoiding it.

I will continue to press for Parliament to sit properly and to fulfill its constitutional role.

Just modernising the old systems would help enormously. We are working with IT infrastructure that is decades out of date in some cases. Processing times are slow. Information does not flow between departments as it should. Staff waste time on manual processes that should be automated.

The ad hoc payments from the Treasury to tide us over are not a sustainable solution. They create uncertainty. They make long-term planning difficult. They leave us constantly scrambling to make budgets work.

What we need is a fundamental reform of local government finance. That means looking at how revenues are raised, how they are distributed, how flexibility and accountability are balanced. The current system was designed for a different era and it no longer fits our circumstances.

The Secretary of State has rightly spelled out the downsides of the current arrangements. What I want to see now is action to fix them. Not another review or consultation, but concrete reform.

Local authorities are delivering essential services to communities. We deserve a funding system that is adequate, predictable, and fair. Local authorities deserve a funding system that is adequate, predictable, and fair. We have been making the case for reform for years. Now we need the government to act.

Our communities depend on the services we provide. We cannot provide them adequately without proper funding.

It is always entertaining to watch Fianna Fáil pretend to be an opposition party despite two years of the confidence and supply agreement that has kept Fine Gael in power and has allowed government policies to continue unchallenged.

The confidence and supply agreement has provided stable government, which has value. But it has also meant that the official opposition has been compromised. They vote with the government on budgets and on confidence matters. They support the overall policy direction. Yet they come into this chamber and criticise as though they bear no responsibility.

The worsening health crisis and housing crisis have happened on their watch as well as on Fine Gael's watch. They have had the power to bring down the government and force an election if they truly disagreed with the direction of policy. They have chosen not to exercise that power.

So when Fianna Fáil deputies rise to criticise waiting lists or homelessness figures, I have to ask: where were you? You have been supporting the government that produced these outcomes. You bear responsibility.

I understand the political calculation. They want to be seen as opposing without actually opposing. They want to criticise without risking an election they might not win. They vote with the government on budgets and confidence matters. They are complicit in the policies they now criticise. Their opposition is performance, not substance.

If they want to be taken seriously as opposition, they should actually oppose rather than enabling the government while pretending to criticise it.

Tomorrow will mark two weeks since Aisling Murphy was attacked and murdered in Tullamore. Her death has shocked the nation and has focused attention on the epidemic of violence against women that we face as a society.

I welcome the fact that we are still discussing this issue two weeks later. Too often, there is a brief moment of outrage after a tragedy, and then attention moves on. The conversation fades. Nothing changes. We cannot allow that to happen this time.

We have to ensure that this conversation leads to action. Real, sustained action to address violence against women. That means properly resourcing specialist services for victims. It means education starting from a young age about consent and respect. It means criminal justice reforms so that perpetrators are held accountable.

It also means looking at the underlying attitudes and structures that perpetuate violence. Misogyny is not just individual bad behaviour. It is cultural and systemic. We need to challenge it at every level.

Women should be able to walk alone, run alone, exist in public spaces without fear. That should not be a radical demand. It should be a basic expectation. Aisling Murphy's death should be a turning point. We cannot let this moment pass without action. We owe it to her memory and to all women to create a society where violence against women is not tolerated.

That requires sustained commitment and concrete action, not just expressions of concern that fade when the headlines move on.

I appreciate the point that the hon. Gentleman is making. I cannot promise to kick shins, as that would be unparliamentary and potentially assault. I find that other methods are more effective for maintaining order and decorum in this chamber.

The stiletto heel comment was meant humorously, but I should clarify that I do not intend physical intimidation of any kind. My tools as Speaker are procedural and rhetorical, not physical.

What I can promise is that I will use all the powers available to me to ensure that this chamber functions properly, that members are treated with respect, that debate is orderly and productive. When members violate the rules or treat the House with contempt, I will respond firmly.

The challenge is balancing order with allowing robust debate. This is a chamber where strong feelings and disagreements are expressed. That is healthy. That is democracy. But there are limits, and it is my job to enforce them.

I appreciate members who work with me to maintain standards. It is not my chamber. It is all of ours. We all have a responsibility to uphold its dignity and its function. I appreciate the point but I clarify that my methods are procedural and rhetorical, not physical. This chamber functions through rules and norms, not through intimidation.

I will enforce the rules fairly and firmly. That is my commitment to all members.

Trust in planning is earned through democratic process. Elected representatives set objectives in national, regional, county, and local development plans. Those plans reflect the will of the people as expressed through elections and through public participation.

The public has multiple opportunities to shape these plans. There are consultation periods. There are public submissions. There are oral hearings. This is deliberative democracy in action, with extensive opportunity for input and for holding decision-makers accountable.

When that process is followed properly, when plans are developed transparently with genuine consultation, they deserve to be respected and implemented. Communities have invested time and energy. They have engaged in good faith. Their voices should matter.

What undermines trust is when that process is overridden or ignored. When plans are developed through proper democratic channels but then set aside for political expediency or developer pressure. When communities discover that their participation was performative, that decisions were already made.

We need to strengthen protections for democratically adopted plans. We need to ensure that public participation is genuine, not just box-ticking. We need accountability when plans are not followed. When democratic processes are followed properly and plans are adopted, they should be respected. Trust is earned through respecting the democratic process, not by overriding it.

We need to protect democratic planning from arbitrary interference.

I thank the hon. Lady for her intervention. She is raising an important concern about how the amendment could be interpreted in practice. That is the kind of constructive scrutiny that improves legislation.

Her point is that the amendment, while well-intentioned, could have the unintended consequence of encouraging abortions outside regulated premises. I understand that concern. We need to be very careful that in trying to protect rights or expand access, we do not create situations that put women at risk.

Regulated premises exist for good reasons. They ensure medical standards are met. They provide safety and oversight. They protect women's health. Any move away from that requirement needs to be thought through very carefully in terms of implications and safeguards.

I do not believe it is necessarily the hon. Lady's intention to suggest that the amendment's supporters want unsafe abortions. But the potential consequence is something that should be addressed. Perhaps there are ways to achieve the amendment's goals while maintaining appropriate medical oversight.

This is complex legislation dealing with sensitive issues. We need to listen to different perspectives and work together to get it right. The amendment raises legitimate concerns that deserve to be addressed. We need to think carefully about how to protect rights and expand access while maintaining appropriate safeguards.

This is complex legislation on sensitive issues. We need to work together to get it right.

One does not need to be a firefighter to understand basic cause and effect. When you pour gasoline on a fire, the fire gets bigger. That is exactly what the Liberal government has done with this policy.

They have identified a problem, and their solution is to do more of what caused the problem in the first place. That is not leadership. That is not problem-solving. That is ideology overriding common sense.

I served as a volunteer firefighter in my community. I learned that you have to understand what is burning and what will extinguish it. You do not just throw resources at a fire randomly. You assess, you plan, you act strategically.

The same principles apply to governing. You need to diagnose problems accurately. You need to understand what interventions will work. You need to be willing to change course when something is not working.

What we are seeing instead is doubling down on failed policies. More spending, more intervention, more of the same approaches that have not produced results. And when critics point this out, the government dismisses them as lacking compassion or not understanding the problem.

I understand the problem perfectly well. What I do not understand is why the government keeps doing things that make it worse. The government keeps doing things that exacerbate problems rather than solving them. That is not governance. That is ideological blindness to evidence and outcomes.

Canadians deserve better than policies that make problems worse while claiming to help.

Since I have the time available, I will elaborate on the issue I raised. I have had extensive discussions with stakeholders about this project. I have met with local representatives, with business interests, with community groups. There is significant interest and also significant concern.

The project has enormous potential. Done properly, it could be transformative for the region. It could create jobs, attract investment, demonstrate innovation. Those are real benefits that we should pursue.

But there are also legitimate questions and concerns that need to be addressed. Environmental impacts. Infrastructure requirements. Community consultation. Funding and financing. These are not obstacles to be dismissed. They are important considerations that need proper attention.

We need to consider this matter comprehensively, not just as it relates to one narrow aspect. Too often, major projects are evaluated in silos. We look at one dimension and miss the broader picture. Then we are surprised when implementation runs into problems we should have anticipated.

What I want to see is a thorough, integrated assessment that considers all relevant factors. Then we can make an informed decision about whether and how to proceed. These are not obstacles to be dismissed. They are important considerations that need proper attention and resolution before we can proceed confidently.

Comprehensive assessment is the foundation for good decision-making.

If Edward VIII had remained as monarch through the Second World War and had been working with Neville Chamberlain, British history would have taken a very different course. I can perfectly well imagine scenarios where different decisions were made about appeasement, about whether to fight, about our relationship with Nazi Germany.

This is not idle speculation. We know Edward VIII's sympathies and associations. We know his views on various political matters. Had he remained king, those views would have influenced events. The counterfactual is sobering.

The point I am making is that individual leaders matter enormously, especially in moments of crisis. The decisions that Churchill made, the leadership he provided, were not inevitable. Someone else in that position might have made different choices.

We should be grateful for the leadership we had when we needed it. We should also be conscious that we cannot assume good leadership will always emerge when required. It depends on who is in office, on their character and judgment, on their advisers and the information they receive.

That is why our institutions and our democratic processes matter so much. They shape who rises to leadership and they constrain what leaders can do. Individual leaders matter enormously. The decisions Churchill made shaped history. Someone else might have made different choices with catastrophic results.

We should be grateful for the leadership we had and conscious that good leadership is not guaranteed.

I believe I understand the member's question. He has characterised our response as backing down, but I would frame it differently. What we did was listen to what the committee sought to convey regarding religious officiants.

Listening and responding to concerns is not weakness. It is how good legislation is made. The committee raised thoughtful points about the implications for religious freedom and for religious organisations' autonomy. We took those points seriously.

We recognised the recommendation regarding maintaining protections for religious officiants who do not wish to perform certain ceremonies. That recommendation reflects a balance between competing rights and interests.

The question is how to ensure that individuals have access to the services and recognition they are entitled to while also respecting religious organisations' autonomy and beliefs. That is not a simple question and there is no perfect answer.

What we have tried to do is find a workable compromise that respects both sets of concerns. Some will say we have gone too far, others that we have not gone far enough. That is the nature of compromise on contentious issues. Listening and responding to concerns is how good legislation is made. We have tried to find a balance that respects competing rights and values.

Some will say we have compromised too much. Others will say not enough. That is the nature of addressing contentious issues in a diverse democracy.

I will now address the Minister of State's contribution directly. I welcome the fact that he has indicated his Department's willingness to take action on this matter. That is encouraging and it is more than we have heard from some other relevant departments.

He mentioned several other government departments that have roles to play here: Education, Health, Housing, others. That is absolutely correct. This is not an issue that falls neatly within one department's remit. It requires cross-government coordination and action.

But that is also where things often break down. When multiple departments are involved, there is a risk that everyone assumes someone else is leading. Responsibility diffuses. Issues fall through cracks. Nothing actually happens despite everyone agreeing something should happen.

What I would urge is that the Minister of State's Department takes a coordinating role. Someone needs to drive this forward, to convene the relevant departments, to set timelines, to hold people accountable for delivering their pieces. Otherwise, we will be having this same conversation in a year with nothing changed.

The willingness to act is necessary but not sufficient. We need structures and processes that ensure action actually follows from good intentions. The Minister's willingness to act is necessary but not sufficient. We need structures that ensure action actually follows.

Someone needs to coordinate across departments and drive implementation. Otherwise, good intentions will not translate into results.

Sustainability is fundamentally about considering the impact of today's decisions on future generations. That is a principle that should inform every domain of policy, not just environmental policy where the term is typically invoked.

When we make decisions about budgets and spending, we should ask: what burden are we placing on future taxpayers? When we make decisions about infrastructure, we should ask: will this serve the needs of the next generation or only our own? When we make decisions about education, we should ask: are we preparing young people for the future they will inhabit?

This requires a longer time horizon than politics usually operates on. Electoral cycles incentivise short-term thinking. Make promises that pay off before the next election. Push costs into the future. That is politically rational but it is not sustainable.

We need institutional mechanisms that force longer-term thinking. Independent fiscal councils that assess long-term impacts. Environmental assessments that consider cumulative effects over decades. Impact assessments for all major legislation that project effects on future generations.

The concept is most developed in environmental policy, and rightly so. Climate change is the paradigmatic sustainability challenge: actions today have consequences decades and centuries into the future. Sustainability means thinking beyond electoral cycles and considering impacts on future generations. That should inform every domain of policy.

We need institutional mechanisms that force longer-term thinking and that hold us accountable for our legacy.

Time is defeating me and I want to ensure the Minister has adequate time to respond to the points that have been raised. Parliamentary time is limited and I do not want to monopolise it, so let me conclude my remarks.

My right hon. Friend the Member for Bournemouth East, who is the new Chairman of the Defence Committee, appeared before the Liaison Committee recently. His priorities and his approach to the role are impressive. The Defence Committee will be well served by his leadership.

The Committee's work is essential for parliamentary oversight of defence and for ensuring that our armed forces are properly resourced and supported. The issues we are discussing today will undoubtedly be examined by the Committee in detail.

I look forward to the Committee's reports and to the government's responses. This is how parliamentary scrutiny should work: detailed examination by expert committees, public reporting of findings, government accountability for responding and acting.
