What I would emphasise to the Minister is the importance of engaging constructively with the Committee's work. Provide the information requested. Take recommendations seriously. Explain when and why you disagree. That kind of engagement strengthens both Parliament and government. Parliamentary time is precious. The Minister deserves adequate time to respond. The Defence Committee will provide important oversight.

I look forward to the Committee's work and to the government's constructive engagement with it.

We have significant challenges in terms of managing the transition as health services adapt to new operating models. The Deputy is quite right to identify the need to use private hospitals and primary care facilities strategically.

During the acute phase of the pandemic, we relied heavily on private hospital capacity. That was essential for maintaining services and for creating space for COVID patients. Moving forward, we need to think about how public and private provision work together.

We also need to focus on keeping people out of hospital when that is clinically appropriate and preferred by patients. Many people can be treated in community settings or at home with proper support. That is better for them and it reduces pressure on hospitals.

Primary care facilities, community health centres, outpatient services, all of these need to be strengthened and better integrated with hospital care. Too often, we have siloed systems where hospitals do not communicate effectively with GPs, where patients fall through gaps between services.

When there is overcrowding in hospitals, that is often a symptom of problems elsewhere in the system. People attending emergency departments who should have been seen in primary care. People remaining in hospital who could be discharged if community support was available. We need to think strategically about how public and private provision work together. We need to strengthen primary care and community services. We need integration across the system.

When there is hospital overcrowding, that reflects problems elsewhere that we need to address systematically.

Every year across the country we come together to mark Holocaust Memorial Day. We remember those who were lost in the Holocaust and in subsequent genocides. We hear stories from survivors. We reflect on our responsibility to prevent such atrocities.

This is essential work. Memory is not automatic. It requires active effort to preserve and transmit. As the generation that experienced the Holocaust passes away, that effort becomes more important and more difficult.

We need to hear the retelling of stories, to listen to testimony, to connect with the human reality of what happened. The statistics are overwhelming: six million Jews murdered, along with Roma, disabled people, gay people, political prisoners, others deemed undesirable by the Nazi regime. Behind each number is a person, a family, a community destroyed.

What we learn from Holocaust Memorial Day should inform how we live and how we respond to injustice today. The Holocaust did not happen suddenly. It was the result of incremental steps, of normalised prejudice, of good people standing by.

We have a responsibility to recognise warning signs, to speak out against hate, to defend the vulnerable, to support democratic institutions and the rule of law. Those are not abstract principles. They are practical commitments that require action. Holocaust Memorial Day is essential work to preserve memory and to transmit it to new generations. What we learn should inform how we respond to injustice today.

We have a responsibility to recognise warning signs, to speak out against hate, to defend the vulnerable. Those are not abstract principles. They require action.

I will be splitting my time with the member for South Surrey—White Rock. We have both been following this issue closely and we both have concerns about how the government has handled it.

It has been very interesting to hear the Liberal speakers today, though also frustrating. There is much rhetoric about values and about protecting Canadians, but when you look at the actual substance of what they are proposing, it does not match the rhetoric.

This is a sad day. The Liberals have brought in closure on what is a very important issue that deserves fuller debate. They are cutting off discussion, limiting scrutiny, forcing through legislation without adequate consideration of concerns that have been raised.

Closure should be a tool of last resort when debate has become obstructive or repetitive. That is not the case here. Members have legitimate questions and concerns. Stakeholders are still raising issues. There is more work to be done.

But the government has decided to force the matter to a vote. That tells us something about their priorities and their respect for Parliament. They want this done, whether or not it is done right. This is a sad day because the government has chosen to cut off debate and force through legislation without adequate scrutiny. That is not how Parliament should work.

Closure should be a last resort. This is not that situation.

I announced this morning that the contingents will return home on Tuesday, 16 October. That decision was made after careful consideration of all relevant factors, and I am confident it is the right course of action.

I also announced that personnel who have been delayed in returning home will receive a €1,000 ex gratia payment in recognition of the disruption caused to them and their families. This is appropriate acknowledgment of the sacrifice they have made.

The delay has been difficult for the personnel and for their families. They have been separated longer than expected. Plans have been disrupted. I want them to know that their service is valued and that we recognise the burden that extensions place on them.

The ex gratia payment is not compensation in a legal sense. It is a gesture of appreciation and recognition. I believe it is the right thing to do given the circumstances.

Going forward, we need to ensure that rotations and deployments are managed in ways that minimise disruption. Personnel need to be able to plan their lives with some degree of certainty about when they will be deployed and when they will return. The personnel and their families have made sacrifices. The ex gratia payment recognises that appropriately.

Going forward, we need better management of deployments to minimise disruption and provide certainty.
